यदा पौर्णमास्यामग्नीषोमावुपांशुयाजस्य देवता तदानीमग्नीषोमा यो अद्येति तस्यानुवाक्या । सूचितं चोक्ता देवता इति खंडे । अग्नीषोमा यो अद्य वामान्यं दिवो मातरिश्वा जभार । आ० १. ६. । इति ॥ तामेतां द्वितीयामृचमाह ॥

## Hymn Text

**अग्नी॑षोमा॒ यो अ॒द्य वा॑मि॒दं वचः॑ स॒पर्य॑ति ।**
**तस्मै॑ धत्तं सु॒वीर्यं॒ गवां॒ पोषं॑ स्व॒श्व्य॑म् ॥ २ ॥**

->पदपाठः<-
**अग्नी॑षोमा । यः । अ॒द्य । वाम् । इ॒दम् । वचः॑ । स॒पर्य॑ति ।**
**तस्मै॑ । ध॒त्त॒म् । सु॒ऽवीर्य॑म् । गवा॑म् । पोष॑म् । सु॒ऽअश्व्य॑म् ॥ २ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

हे **अग्नीषोमौ** यो **यजमानोऽद्यास्मिन्कर्मणि वां** युवाभ्यां युष्मदर्थ**मिदं** स्तुतिलक्षणं **वचो** वाक्यं **सपर्यति** । पूजितं करोति । **तस्मै** यजमानाय **गवां** पशूनां **पोषमभिवृद्धिं धत्तं** । प्रयच्छतं । कीदृशं पोषं । **सुवीर्यं** । शोभनेन वीर्येण सामर्थ्येनोपेतं । **स्वश्व्यं** । शोभनैरश्वैर्युक्तं ॥ गवां । सावेकाच इति प्राप्तस्य विभक्त्युदात्तत्वस्य न गोश्वन् साववर्णैति प्रतिषेधः ॥

->तृतीयामृचमाह ॥<-

## Hymn Text

**अग्नी॑षोमा॒ य आहु॑तिं॒ यो वां॑ दा॒शाद्ध॑वि॒ष्कृति॑म् ।**
**स प्र॒जया॑ सु॒वीर्यं॑ वि॒श्वमायु॒र्व्य॑श्नवत् ॥ ३ ॥**

->पदपाठः<-
**अग्नी॑षोमा । यः । आ॒हुति॑म् । यः । वाम् । दाशा॑त् । ह॒विः॒ऽकृति॑म् ।**
**सः । प्र॒ऽजया॑ । सु॒ऽवीर्य॑म् । वि॒श्वम् । आयुः॑ । वि । अ॒श्न॒व॒त् ॥ ३ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

हे **अग्नीषोमौ यो यजमान आहुतिमाज्याहुतिं वां** युवाभ्यां **दाशात्** । दद्यात् । अथवा **हविष्कृतिं** हविषा चरुपुरोडाशादिना कृतामाहुतिं यो यजमानो दद्यात् । **स** यजमानः **प्रजया** पुत्रपौत्रादिना युक्तं **सुवीर्यं** शोभनवीर्ययुक्तं **विश्वं** सर्व**मायु**र्जीवनं **व्यश्नवत्** । व्याप्नोतु ॥ आहुतिं । जुहोतेः क्तिनि तादौ चेति गतेः प्रकृतिस्वरत्वं । दाशात् । दाशृ दाने । लेड्याडागमः । यद्वृत्तयोगादनिघातः । हविष्कृतिं । हविः कृतिः करणं यस्यामाहुतौ । बहुव्रीहौ पूर्वपदप्रकृतिस्वरत्वं ।

1. Agni and Soma, showerers (of desires), favourably hear this my invocation, graciously accept my hymns, and bestow felicity on the donor (of the oblation).

2. Agni and Soma, grant, to him who addresses this prayer to you both, store of cattle with sound strength, and good horses.

3. Agni and Soma, may he who offers you the oblation of clarified butter enjoy sound strength, with progeny, through all his life.

4. Agni and Soma, that prowess of yours, by which you have carried off the cows that were the food of Pani, is (well-) known to us. You have slain the offspring of Brisaya; and you have acquired the one luminary (the sun), for the benefit of the many.

translations.T1:
<meta>continues from previous page: discussing the grammatical derivation of the word for calling or invocation</meta> The suffix <term>ap</term> is added to the root <term>hve</term> <gloss>to call</gloss> with the vocalization of the semi-vowel. For the word <term>sūktāni</term> <gloss>well-spoken hymns</gloss>, the past passive participle suffix <term>kta</term> is added to the root <term>vac</term> <gloss>to speak</gloss> preceded by the prefix <term>su</term> <gloss>well</gloss>. According to the rule that the final syllable of the second member is accented after the prefix <term>su</term>, the accent falls on the end. For <term>haryatam</term> <gloss>desirable</gloss>, the root is <term>harya</term> <gloss>to go or to desire</gloss>, belonging to the first class of roots.

When <term>Agni</term> <gloss>Fire</gloss> and <term>Soma</term> <gloss>the Sacred Libation</gloss> are the designated deities of the <term>upāṃśuyāja</term> <gloss>silent sacrifice</gloss> during the full moon, then the verse beginning with "O Agni and Soma, he who today..." is used as the invitatory prayer <note>original: "anuvākyā"</note>. This is indicated in the section of the ritual manuals stating: "The deities have been mentioned; Agni and Soma, he who today... Matariśvan brought the one from heaven." <note>referencing Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1.6</note>. He now states this second verse.

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, he who today honors you with this speech, for him provide great strength, the increase of cattle, and abundance of good horses.** 2

->Word-for-Word Breakdown<-
**Agni and Soma; who; today; for you two; this; speech; honors; for him; provide; great strength; of cattle; increase; abundance of good horses.** 2

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, whichever **sacrificer** <note>original: "yajamāna"</note> **today**, in this ritual, **honors** or makes worshipful **this speech** or sentence characterized by praise **for you two**. **For him**, the sacrificer, **provide** or grant the **increase** or growth **of cattle** or animals. What kind of increase? **Great strength**, meaning endowed with excellent vigor and power. **Abundance of good horses**, meaning accompanied by excellent horses. Regarding the grammar of "of cattle" <note>original: "gavām"</note>, the rule that would place the accent on the case ending for monosyllabic bases is prohibited here by the specific rule regarding the words for cow and horse.

---

->He now states the third verse.<-

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, he who offers an oblation, or he who prepares a sacrifice for you, may he, through his progeny, enjoy great strength and a full span of life.** 3

->Word-for-Word Breakdown<-
**Agni and Soma; who; oblation; who; for you two; gives; the preparation of sacrifice; he; through progeny; great strength; all; life; [may he] thoroughly enjoy.** 3

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma, whichever sacrificer gives** or offers an **oblation** consisting of clarified butter to you two. Or, whichever sacrificer gives a **preparation of sacrifice**, meaning an offering made of sacrificial cake <note>original: "puroḍāśa"</note> or boiled grains <note>original: "caru"</note>. **He**, the sacrificer, **may enjoy** or attain a **full** or complete **life** along with **progeny**, such as sons and grandsons, and possessing **great strength** or excellent vigor. Regarding "oblation" <note>original: "āhutim"</note>, the suffix <term>ktin</term> is added to the root <term>hu</term> <gloss>to sacrifice</gloss>, and the original accent of the root is preserved. "He gives" <note>original: "dāśāt"</note> comes from the root <term>dāśṛ</term> <gloss>to give</gloss> in the Vedic subjunctive <note>original: "leṭ"</note> with the <term>āḍ</term> augment. The verb does not lose its accent because it is connected to the relative pronoun "who". "Preparation of sacrifice" <note>original: "haviṣkṛtim"</note> refers to an offering in which the preparation <note>original: "kṛti"</note> of the oblation <note>original: "havis"</note> is performed. In this compound <note>original: "bahuvrīhi"</note>, the first member retains its original accent.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...to the root 'hve' (to call), with the suffix 'ap' and the process of 'samprasarana' (vowel substitution). 'Suktani' (well-spoken): formed from 'su' (well) and 'vakti' (to speak) with the 'nishtha' suffix indicating the past participle. By the rule 'supamanat ktah' (the suffix 'kta' after a word indicating a good standard), the final syllable is accented. 'Haryatam': from the root 'hary' (to desire or shine), belonging to the 'bhaunadika' class.</meta>

When the deity of the 'upanshu-yaja' (silent sacrifice) on the full moon is Agni and Soma, then the verse beginning 'Agni-Soma yo adya' serves as the 'anuvakya' (invitation verse). This is indicated in the section titled 'Ukta Devata' (The stated deities). As stated: "O Agni and Soma, he who today...", etc. <note>Aitareya Brahmana 1.6</note>. He now declares this second verse.

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, he who today offers this speech to you two,**
**Bestow upon him great heroic power, prosperity of cattle, and good horses. <note>Verse 2</note>**

->Pada-patha<-
**Agni-Soma | He who | today | to you two | this | speech | honors.**
**To him | bestow | good-heroic-power | of cows | prosperity | good-horsed.**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, the **sacrificer who today, in this ritual, offers this speech** (in the form of a hymn) **to you two**—that is, for your sake—honors you. **Bestow upon that sacrificer prosperity** (growth) **of cows** (cattle). What kind of prosperity? One possessing **good heroic power**, accompanied by excellent strength, and **possessing good horses**. Regarding the word *gavam* (of cows), the accent on the case-ending—which would normally occur due to the rule 'savekach'—is prevented by the rule 'na goshvan savavarnai' (accent is not shifted in certain forms of 'go' and 'ashva').

---

->He now declares the third verse.<-

---

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, he who would give an offering to you, he who would give a sacrifice prepared with oblations,**
**He, with progeny and heroic power, shall attain a full life. <note>Verse 3</note>**

->Pada-patha<-
**Agni-Soma | He who | offering | he who | to you two | would give | oblation-preparation.**
**He | with progeny | good-heroic-power | all | life | attains.**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, **the sacrificer who offers an oblation** (such as clarified butter) **to you two**, or **who offers an oblation prepared with** ritual materials like *charu* (sacrificial porridge) and *purudasha* (sacrificial cake), **that sacrificer**, endowed **with progeny** (sons and grandsons) and **good heroic power**, shall **attain a full life** (the entire span of existence). Regarding the word *ahutim* (offering): by the rule 'juhoteh ktini tadau cha', the radical accent is retained. Regarding *dashat* (would give): from the root *dash* (to give); it takes the 'let' (Vedic subjunctive) augment 'at'. Because it is connected to a relative pronoun, it is not subject to the 'anighata' (lack of accent) rule. Regarding *havishkritim* (oblation-preparation): the act of preparing the oblation. In a *bahuvrihi* compound, the first member retains its original accent.

When the deity of the 'upansuyaga' <note>a silent offering</note> sacrifice is Agni and Soma on the day of the full moon, then the verse beginning 'Agnishoma yo adya' is used as the 'anuvakya' <note>invitatory verse</note>. This is noted in the section titled 'Ukta Devata' <note>Deities Mentioned</note>. ## Hymn Text

**Agni and Soma, whoever today offers this word to you both.**
**For him, bestow good vigor, prosperity in cows, and good horses. <note>verse 2</note>**

->Pada-patha (Word-by-word analysis)<-
**Agni-Soma | who | today | of you two | this | word | serves/honors.**
**For him | bestow | good-vigor | of cows | prosperity | good-horsedness. <note>verse 2</note>**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, the **sacrificer who today in this rite serves you both**, meaning for your sake, [and] performs this **word** characterized by praise, [you both] **bestow upon that** sacrificer **prosperity in cows**, meaning an increase in cattle. What kind of prosperity? **Good vigor**, meaning endowed with excellent power. **Good horses**, meaning endowed with excellent horses. Regarding the word *gavam* (of cows): the rule 'savekac' (regarding the accent of the case ending) would generally apply, but it is prohibited by the rule 'na goshvan savavarnai' <note>a grammatical rule regarding the accentuation of certain nouns</note>.

---

->He speaks of the third verse.<-

---

## Hymn Text

**Agni and Soma, whoever offers an oblation to you both, whoever makes a sacrificial offering.**
**He, with progeny, good vigor, and all [his] life, shall attain success. <note>verse 3</note>**

->Pada-patha (Word-by-word analysis)<-
**Agni-Soma | who | oblation | who | of you two | gives | sacrifice-making.**
**He | with progeny | good-vigor | all | life | attains. <note>verse 3</note>**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma, the sacrificer who offers an oblation**, meaning an offering of clarified butter, to **you both**, or **who offers the sacrificial preparation**, meaning an oblation made with sacrificial food such as 'charu' or 'purodasha' <note>types of rice cakes or grain offerings</note>, **that** sacrificer **with progeny**, meaning children and grandchildren, and **with good vigor**, endowed with excellent strength, **shall attain the whole life**, meaning let him reach the full span of existence. Regarding the word *ahutim*: it is derived from the root 'hu' (to offer) with the 'ktin' suffix, and the accent remains on the radical according to the rule 'tadau ca'. *Dasat*: from the root 'dash' (to give), with the addition of the augment 'at' in the 'let' (Vedic subjunctive) mood. Because it is associated with a relative pronoun, the verb does not lose its accent. *Havishkrtim*: [meaning] that sacrifice in which the preparation of the offering is performed. It is a 'bahuvrihi' compound, and the accent remains on the first member.

# पराभिध्यानात्तु तिरोहितं ततो ह्यस्य बन्धविपर्ययौ ।। 3.2.5 ।।

अथापि स्यात् -- परस्यैव तावदात्मनोंऽशः जीवः -- अग्नेरिव विस्फुलिङ्गः; तत्रैवं सति यथा अग्निविस्फुलिङ्गयोः समाने दहनप्रकाशनशक्ती भवतः, एवं जीवेश्वरयोरपि ज्ञानैश्वर्यशक्ती; ततश्च जीवस्य ज्ञानैश्वर्यवशात् सांकल्पिकी स्वप्ने रथादिसृष्टिर्भविष्यतीति। अत्रोच्यते -- सत्यपि जीवेश्वरयोरंशांशिभावे प्रत्यक्षमेव जीवस्येश्वरविपरीतधर्मत्वम्। किं पुनर्जीवस्य ईश्वरसमानधर्मत्वं नास्त्येव? न नास्त्येव; विद्यमानमपि तत् तिरोहितम् अविद्यादिव्यवधानात्। तत्पुनस्तिरोहितं सत् परमेश्वरमभिध्यायतो यतमानसय जन्तोर्विधूतध्वान्तस्य -- तिमिरतिरस्कृतेव दृक्शक्तिः औषधवीर्यात् -- ईश्वरप्रसादात् संसिद्धस्य कस्यचिदेवाविर्भवति, न स्वभावत एव, सर्वेषां जन्तूनाम्; कुतः? ततो हि ईश्वराद्धेतोः, अस्य जीवस्य, बन्धमोक्षौ भवतः -- ईश्वरस्वरूपापरिज्ञानात् बन्धः, तत्स्वरूपपरिज्ञानात्तु मोक्षः। तथा च श्रुतिः -- 'ज्ञात्वा देवं सर्वपाशापहानिः क्षीणैः क्लेशैर्जन्ममृत्युप्रहाणिः। तस्याभिध्यानात्तृतीयं देहभेदे विश्वैश्वर्यं केवल आप्तकामः' इत्येवमाद्या ।।

# देहयोगाद्वा सोऽपि ।। 3.2.6 ।।

।। 3.2.6 ।।

कस्मात्पुनर्जीवः परमात्मांश एव सन् तिरस्कृतज्ञानैश्वर्यो भवति? युक्तं तु ज्ञानैश्वर्ययोरातिरस्कृतत्वम्, विस्फुलिङ्गस्येव दहनप्रकाशनयोः -- इति। उच्यते -- सत्यमेवैतत्; सोऽपि तु जीवस्य ज्ञानैश्वर्यतिरोभावः, देहयोगात् देहेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिविषयवेदनादियोगात् भवति। अस्ति च अत्रोपमा -- यथा अग्नेर्दहनप्रकाशनसंपन्नस्याप्यरणिगतस्य दहनप्रकाशने तिरोहिते भवतः, यथा वा भस्मच्छन्नस्य -- एवमविद्याप्रत्युपस्थापितनामरूपकृतदेहपाधियोगात् तद्विवेकभ्रमकृतो जीवस्य ज्ञानैश्वर्यतिरोभावः। वा-शब्दो जीवस्य ईश्वरात् अन्यत्वशङ्काव्यावृत्त्यर्थः। नन्वन्य एव जीवः ईश्वरादस्तु, तिरस्कृतज्ञानैश्वर्यत्वात्; किं देहयोगकल्पनया? नेत्युच्यते -- न हि अन्यत्वं जीवस्य ईश्वरादुपपद्यते -- 'सेयं देवतैक्षत' इत्युपक्रम्य 'अनेन जीवेनात्मनानुप्रविश्य' इत्यात्मशब्देन जीवस्य परामर्शात्; 'तत् सत्यं स आत्मा तत्त्वमसि श्वेतकेतो' इति च जीवाय उपदिशति ईश्वरत्वम्; अतः अनन्य एव ईश्वराञ्जीवः सन् देहयोगात्तिरोहितज्ञानैश्वर्यो भवति। अतश्च न सांकल्पिकी जीवस्य स्वप्ने रथादिसृष्टिर्घटते; यदि च सांकल्पिकी स्वप्ने रथादिसृष्टिः स्यात्, नैवानिष्टं कश्चित्स्वप्नं पश्येत्, न हि कश्चिदृनिष्टं संकल्पयते। यत्पुनरुक्तम् -- जागरितदेशश्रुतिः स्वप्नस्य सत्यत्वं ख्यापयतीति, न तत्साम्यवचनं सत्यत्वाभिप्रायम्, स्वयंज्योतिष्ट्वविरोधात्, श्रुत्यैव च स्वप्ने रथाद्यभावस्य दर्शितत्वात्; जागरितप्रभववासनानिमित्तत्वात् स्वप्नस्य तत्तुल्यनिर्भासत्वाभिप्रायं तत्। तस्मादुपपन्नं स्वप्नस्य मायामात्रत्वम् ।।

# तदभावो नाडीषु तच्छ्रुतेरात्मनि च ।। 3.2.7 ।।

तदभावाधिकरणम् ।। 3.2.7 ।।

स्वप्नावस्था परीक्षिता; सुषुप्तावस्थेदानीं परीक्ष्यते। तत्रैताः सुषुप्तविषयाः श्रुतयो भवन्ति; क्वचिच्छूयते -- 'तद्यत्रैतत्सुप्तः समस्तः संप्रसन्नः स्वप्नं न विजानात्यासु तदा नाडीषु सुप्तो भवति' इति; अन्यत्र तु नाडीरेवानुक्रम्य श्रूयते -- 'ताभिः प्रत्यवसृप्य पुरीतति शेते' इति; तथान्यत्र नाडीरेवानुक्रम्य -- 'तासु तदा भवति यदा सुप्तः स्वप्नं न कंचन पश्यत्यथास्मिन्प्राण एवैकधा भवति' इति; तथान्यत्र -- 'य एषोऽन्तर्हृदय आकाशस्तस्मिञ्छेते' इति; तथान्यत्र -- 'सतासोम्य तदा संपन्नो भवति स्वमपीतो भवति' इति; तथा -- 'प्राज्ञेनात्मना संपरिष्वक्तो न बाह्यं किंचन वेद नान्तरम्' इति च ।।

5. But by the meditation on the highest that which is hidden (viz. the equality of the Lord and the soul, becomes manifest) ; for from him (the Lord) are its (the soul's) bondage and release.

Well, but the individual soul is a part of the highest Self as the spark is a part of the fire. And as fire and spark have in common the powers of burning and giving light, so the individual soul and the Lord have in common the powers of knowledge and rulership ; hence the individual soul may, by means of its lordship, effect in the dreaming state a creation of chariots and the like, springing from its wishes (sawkalpa). — To this we reply that although the Lord and the individual soul stand to each other in the relation of whole and part, yet it is manifest to perception that the attributes of the two are of a different nature. — Do you then mean to say that the individual soul has no common attributes with the Lord ? — We do not maintain that ; but we say that the equality of attributes, although existing, is hidden by the veil of Nescience. In the case of some persons indeed who strenuously meditate on the Lord and who, their ignorance being dispelled at last, obtain through the favour of the Lord extraordinary powers and insight, that hidden equality becomes manifest— just as through the action of strong medicines the power of sight of a blind man becomes manifest ; but it does not on its own account reveal itself to all men. — Why not? — Because 'from him,' i.e. from the Lord there are bondage and release of it, viz. the individual soul. That means : bondage is due to the absence of knowledge of the Lord's true nature ; release is due to the presence of such knowledge. Thus 5ruti declares, ' When that god is known all fetters fall off; sufferings are destroyed and birth and death cease. From meditating on him there arises, on the dissolution of the body, a third state, that of universal Lordship ; he who is alone is satisfied ' (5vet. Up. I, ii), and similar passages.

6. Or that (viz. the concealment of the soul's pov^ers springs) from its connexion with the body.

But if the soul is a part of the highest Self, why should its knowledge and lordship be hidden ? We should rather expect them to be as manifest as the light and the heat of the spark. — True, we reply ; but the state of concealment of the soul's knowledge and lordship is due to its being joined to a body, i.e. to a body, sense-organs, mind, buddhi, sense-objectSj sensations, &c. And to this state of things there applies the simile : As the heat and light of the fire are hidden as long as the fire is still hidden in the wood from which it will be produced by friction, or as long as it is covered by ashes ; so, in consequence of the soul being connected with limiting adjuncts in the form of a body, &c., founded on name and form as presented by Nescience, its knowledge and lordship remain hidden as long as it is possessed by the erroneous notion of not being distinct from those adjuncts. — The word ' or ' in the Sutra is meant to discard the suspicion that the Lord and the soul might be separate entities. — But why should not the soul be separate from the Lord considering the state of concealment of its knowledge and power? If we allow the two to be fundamentally separate, we need not assume that their separateness is due to the soul's connexion with the body. — It is impossible, we reply, to assume the soul to be separate froni the Lord. For in the scriptural passage beginning with 'That divinity thought' &c. (K/i. Up. "VI, 3, 2) we meet with the clause, ' It entered into those beings with this living Self (^iva atman) ; where the individual soul is referred to as the Self. And then we have the other passage, ' It is the True ; it is the Self ; that art thou, O 5vetaketu,' which again teaches that the Lord is the Self of the soul. Hence the soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and power are obscured by its connexion with the body. From this it follows that the dreaming soul is not able to create, from its mere wishes, chariots and other things. If the soul possessed that power, nobody would ever have an unpleasant dream ; for nobody ever wishes for something unpleasant to himself. — We finally deny that the scriptural passage about the waking state (' dream is the same as the place of waking ' &c.) indicates the reality of dreams. The statement made there about the equality of the two states is not meant to indicate that dreams are real, for that would conflict with the soul's self-luminousness (referred to above), and scripture, moreover, expressly declares that the chariots, &c., of a dream have no real existence ; it merely means that dreams, because due to mental impressions (vasana) received in the waking state, are equal to the latter in appearance.— From all this it follows that dreams are mere illusion.

7. The absence of that (i.e. of dreams, i.e. dreamless sleep) takes place in the na^^is and in the Self; according to scriptural statement.

The state of dream has been discussed ; we are now going to enquire into the state of deep sleep. A number of scriptural passages refer to that state. In one place we read, ' When a man is asleep, reposing and at perfect rest so that he sees no dream, then he has entered into those na^is' [Kh. Up. VIII, 6, 3). In another place it is said with reference to the na^is, ' Through them he moves forth and rests in the surrounding body' (BW. Up. II, i, 19). So also in another place, ' In these the person is when sleeping he sees no dream. Then he becomes one with the prawa alone' (Kau. Up. IV, 20). Again in another place, 'That ether which is within the heart in that he reposes ' (Br/. Up. IV, 4, 22). Again, ' Then he becomes united with that which is ; he is gone to his Self {Kh. Up. VI, 8, i). And, ' Embraced by the highest Self (pra^/^a) he knows nothing that is without, nothing that is within' (B/-/. Up. IV, 3, 21). Here the doubt arises whether the na^is, &c., mentioned in the above passages are independent from each other and constitute various places for the soul in the state of deep sleep, or if they stand in mutual relation so as to constitute one such place only. The purvapakshin takes the former view on account of the various places mentioned serving one and the same purpose. Things serving the same purpose, as, e.g. rice and barley, are never seen to be dependent on each other.

# But from meditating on the Supreme, that which is obscured; from that, the bondage and liberation of this one occur. 3.2.5.

It might be argued: The individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual consciousness</gloss>) is merely a part of the Supreme Self, like a spark from a fire. If this is so, just as the spark shares the same power of burning and illuminating as the fire, the individual soul and the Lord (<term>ishvara</term> <gloss>the Supreme Ruler</gloss>) must share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, through the power of its knowledge and sovereignty, the individual soul would be able to create chariots and other objects in a dream through mere will. 

To this, we reply: While the relationship between the individual soul and the Lord is that of part and whole, the individual soul's possession of qualities opposite to those of the Lord is a matter of direct experience. Does this mean the individual soul lacks the qualities of the Lord entirely? No, it does not lack them. Though they exist, they are obscured by the veil of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>primordial ignorance</gloss>) and similar factors. 

This obscured power manifests only in a being who strives, who meditates on the Supreme Lord, and whose darkness has been dispelled—just as the power of sight, obscured by a cataract, becomes clear through the strength of medicine. It manifests through the grace of the Lord, not by nature for all beings. Why? Because it is from that cause, the Lord, that the bondage and liberation of this soul occur; bondage arises from not knowing the nature of the Lord, and liberation arises from knowing that nature. Thus, the scripture says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. Through meditation on Him, the third state <note>referring to the state beyond waking and dreaming</note> is attained at the dissolution of the body, where one becomes the master of all and reaches all desires."

# Or it is so because of connection with a body. 3.2.6.

Why is the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, one whose knowledge and sovereignty are obscured? It is logical that these powers should remain unobscured, as the power of a spark to burn and illuminate remains. We respond: This is true. However, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of its connection with a body—the connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. 

There is an analogy here: just as the burning and illuminating powers of fire, even though present, become obscured when the fire is contained within a piece of wood, or covered by ashes, so too does the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occur due to its connection with the body, which is composed of names and forms created by ignorance, and the resulting confusion of identity. The word "or" <term>va</term> is used to address the doubt regarding the soul being distinct from the Lord. 

If one suggests that the soul is indeed distinct from the Lord because its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured, and that we need not postulate a connection to a body, we say: No. The distinctness of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. The text begins with "That Deity perceived" and continues, "I shall enter these beings with this individual soul" <note>original: "Anena jivenatmana anupravishya"</note>, referring to the soul as the Self. Furthermore, it instructs the soul in its divinity: "That is the Truth, that is the Self, you are That, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but it becomes one whose knowledge and sovereignty are obscured due to its connection with a body. 

Because of this, the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream by the soul's will is not possible. If the creation in a dream were merely by will, no one would see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is undesirable. As for the argument that the experience of the waking world proves the reality of the dream world, that comparison is not intended to suggest reality, as it would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and such in a dream. That comparison simply means the dream is similar to the waking state because it is caused by impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious tendencies</gloss>) resulting from waking experiences. Therefore, the conclusion that the dream is mere illusion (<term>maya-matra</term> <gloss>only an appearance</gloss>) is well-founded.

# Its absence is in the channels, the heart-membrane, and the Self, according to scripture. 3.2.7.

The Section on its Absence.

The state of dreaming has been examined. Now, the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>dreamless sleep</gloss>) is examined. There are various scriptural passages regarding deep sleep. In one place, it is heard: "When this person is asleep, having become completely serene, and knows no dream, he has entered these channels (<term>nadi</term> <gloss>subtle energy channels</gloss>)." In another place, having mentioned the channels, it is heard: "Having moved through them, he rests in the heart-membrane (<term>puritat</term> <gloss>the pericardium</gloss>)." Elsewhere, after mentioning the channels: "He abides in them when he is asleep and sees no dreams; then he becomes one with the vital force (<term>prana</term> <gloss>life breath</gloss>)." Elsewhere: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Elsewhere: "O gentle one, then he becomes united with the Pure Being, he attains his own nature." And also: "Embraced by the intelligent Self, he knows nothing external or internal." 

Here is the doubt: Are these—the channels and the rest—separate places for deep sleep, independent of one another, or is there one place for deep sleep, with them being mutually dependent? What is the initial position? They are separate, because they serve the same purpose, and things serving the same purpose are not usually mutually dependent...

<summary>This passage discusses why the individual soul's divine powers of knowledge and sovereignty remain obscured, attributing this state to the soul's connection with a physical body and ignorance, while affirming the soul's fundamental non-difference from the Supreme Self (Brahman). It then introduces the topic of deep sleep, posing the question of whether the various scriptural descriptions of where the soul resides during sleep are separate or unified locations.</summary>

VI, 8, i). And, ' Embraced by the highest Self (pra^/^a) he knows nothing that is without, nothing that is within' (B/-/. Up. IV, 3, 21). Here the doubt arises whether the na^is, &c., mentioned in the above passages are independent from each other and constitute various places for the soul in the state of deep sleep, or if they stand in mutual relation so as to constitute one such place only. The purvapakshin takes the former view on account of the various places mentioned serving one and the same purpose. Things serving the same purpose, as, e.g. rice and barley, are never seen to be dependent on each other.
translations.T3:
# But by meditating on the Highest, that which is hidden is revealed, for from Him come bondage and liberation. (3.2.5)

3.2.5

One might argue: the individual soul <term>jiva</term> <gloss>the living being or individual self</gloss> is a part of the Highest Self, just as a spark is a part of a fire. Since this is so, just as the fire and the spark share the same powers of burning and lighting, the individual soul and the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>the Supreme Ruler or God</gloss> must share the same powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Therefore, by the force of this knowledge and sovereignty, the individual soul should be able to create chariots and other objects in dreams merely by volition.

To this we reply: Even though there is a relationship of part and whole between the individual soul and the Lord, it is a matter of direct perception that the soul possesses characteristics opposite to those of the Lord.

Does this mean the soul has no common characteristics with the Lord at all? No, that is not the case. Although these powers exist, they are hidden <term>tirohita</term> <gloss>concealed or obscured</gloss> due to the interference of ignorance <term>avidya</term> and other factors. However, that which is hidden becomes manifest in someone who has shaken off the darkness of ignorance through the meditation on the Supreme Lord and through intense effort. Just as sight, though obstructed by a cataract, can be restored by the power of medicine, this manifestation occurs by the grace of the Lord in one who has attained perfection. It does not happen naturally for all living beings.

Why? Because from Him <note>referring to the Lord</note> come both the bondage and the liberation of this individual soul. Bondage results from the lack of knowledge of the Lord’s true nature, while liberation results from the realization of that nature. As the scripture <term>shruti</term> <gloss>sacred revealed text</gloss> says: By knowing God, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of afflictions, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, a third state is reached upon the dissolution of the body: universal sovereignty, where one is absolute and has all desires fulfilled. <note>original: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note>

# Or that concealment results from connection with the body. (3.2.6)

3.2.6

Why then does the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It would seem more logical for these qualities not to be hidden, just as the burning and light of a spark are not hidden.

We reply: This is true, yet the concealment of the soul’s knowledge and power occurs because of its connection with the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the power of fire to burn and illuminate is hidden when it is latent within a piece of wood <note>arani: wood used for friction-fire</note>, or when it is covered by ashes, similarly, due to the connection with the limiting conditions of the body and mind created by the names and forms of ignorance, the soul's power is obscured by the delusion of failing to distinguish itself from them.

The word or in the verse serves to dispel the doubt that the soul is fundamentally different from the Lord. One might ask: Why not just say the soul is entirely different from the Lord because its powers are obscured, rather than imagining a connection with the body?

We say no, because the difference of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. Starting with the passage "That divinity thought," the text continues "Entering with this living self," using the word "self" to refer to the individual soul. Furthermore, the text "That is the Truth, that is the Self, Thou Art That, O Shvetaketu" teaches that the individual soul is identical with the Lord.

Therefore, the individual soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden by the connection with the body. Consequently, it is not possible for the soul to create chariots in dreams by mere volition. If dream-creation were truly volitional, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is unpleasant for themselves.

Regarding the point made earlier that the scripture compares the dream state to the waking state to show dreams are real: that comparison is not intended to suggest reality. It would contradict the soul's nature as "self-luminous" and the scriptural statement that there are no actual chariots in dreams. The comparison is meant to show that dreams appear similar to waking life because they are caused by the impressions <term>vasanas</term> left over from the waking state. Thus, it is established that the dream state is mere illusion <term>maya-matra</term>.

# The absence of that dream occurs in the channels and in the Self, according to the scripture. (3.2.7)

The Section on the Absence of Dreams (3.2.7)

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep <term>sushupti</term> is examined. Regarding deep sleep, there are several scriptural passages. In one place it says: When he is thus asleep, composed, and serene, and knows no dream, he then sleeps in these channels <term>nadis</term>. <note>Chhandogya Upanishad 8.6.3</note> Elsewhere, following a description of the channels, it says: Through them he creeps back and rests in the pericardium <term>puritat</term>. <note>Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.1.19</note> Similarly, in another place: In these he remains when he is asleep and sees no dream; then he becomes one with the vital breath <term>prana</term> alone. <note>Kaushitaki Upanishad 4.19</note> Elsewhere: He sleeps in the space within the heart. <note>Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.1.17</note> Also: Then, my dear, he becomes united with the Truly Existing; he has gone to his own Self. <note>Chhandogya Upanishad 6.8.1</note> And: Embraced by the conscious Self, he knows nothing without and nothing within. <note>Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.21</note>

The doubt arises here: Are these various locations like the channels and so on independent of each other as separate places for deep sleep, or do they together constitute a single place of sleep in relation to one another?

What is the initial view? That they are separate. Why? Because they serve the same purpose. Things that serve the same purpose are usually not dependent on one another...

<summary>Shankara explains that the individual soul's divine powers are obscured by its identification with the body and ignorance. He also begins a discussion on deep sleep, questioning whether the various scriptural locations for sleep function independently or together.</summary>

# But because of contemplation of the Supreme, that which is veiled; for from Him are the bondage and freedom of this one. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued: the individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>the embodied soul</gloss>) is but a part of the Supreme Self (<term>Paramatman</term> <gloss>the Supreme Self</gloss>), just as a spark is of fire. If this is so, then just as the spark and the fire share the same power of burning and illumination, so too should the <term>jiva</term> and the Lord (<term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>the Supreme Ruler</gloss>) share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty (<term>jnana-aishvarya</term> <gloss>omniscience and omnipotence</gloss>). Consequently, by virtue of these powers, the <term>jiva</term> should be able to create chariots and the like in dreams through mere will. 

To this, we reply: even though the <term>jiva</term> and <term>Ishvara</term> stand in the relation of part and whole, the <term>jiva</term>’s nature is observed to be the opposite of the Lord’s. Does this mean the <term>jiva</term> possesses no attributes equal to the Lord? It is not that they do not exist; they are merely veiled by the obstacles of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance/nescience</gloss>) and the like. This veiled state disappears only for those who meditate upon the Supreme Lord, those who strive, and those whose darkness has been dispelled—just as the power of sight, obstructed by a cataract, becomes manifest through the potency of medicine—or through the grace of the Lord. It does not manifest naturally in all beings. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, proceed the bondage and liberation of this soul: bondage arises from lack of knowledge of His nature, and liberation arises from knowledge of His nature. As the <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>Vedic scripture</gloss> says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death are left behind. By contemplating Him, upon the separation of the body, one attains the third state, the sovereignty of the universe, and all desires are fulfilled."

# Or because of the connection with the body. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why, then, does the <term>jiva</term>, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty veiled? It would be reasonable for these powers to remain unveiled, as the burning and illumination are in a spark. 

We reply: that is true; however, this veiling of the <term>jiva</term>’s knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of the connection with the body, which includes the senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the power of burning and light in fire—though naturally present—remains hidden when the fire is contained within fuel, or when it is covered by ash, so too is the <term>jiva</term>’s knowledge and sovereignty obscured by the connection to the body produced by name and form, which are conjured by <term>avidya</term>. The word "or" (<term>va</term>) is used to exclude the doubt that the <term>jiva</term> is distinct from the Lord. One might ask, "Let the <term>jiva</term> be distinct from the Lord, as its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why posit a connection to the body?" 

We respond: it is not possible for the <term>jiva</term> to be distinct from the Lord. For scripture, having introduced the subject with "That Divinity willed," continues, "I shall enter into these beings with this living self (<term>jiva atman</term>)," indicating the <term>jiva</term> with the word "Self." Furthermore, it instructs the <term>jiva</term> on its own divine nature, saying, "That is the truth, that is the Self, that thou art, O Svetaketu." Therefore, the <term>jiva</term> is identical to the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are veiled due to the body. Hence, the creation of chariots and such in dreams by the <term>jiva</term> through mere will is not possible. If it were a matter of mere will, no one would see an undesirable dream, for no one wills what is undesirable. 

Regarding the claim that the scripture describing the waking state confirms the reality of the dream state, that comparison is not meant to imply equal reality, as it would contradict the fact that the soul is self-luminous. The scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and the like in dreams. That comparison only means that the dream is similar to the waking state in that it is caused by impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>latent impressions/tendencies</gloss>) arising from the waking state. Therefore, it is established that the dream state is mere illusion (<term>maya-matra</term> <gloss>consisting only of illusion</gloss>).

# The absence of that is in the subtle channels, because of that scriptural statement, and in the Self. || 3.2.7 ||

The section on the absence of that. || 3.2.7 ||

The dream state has been examined; now the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>deep dreamless sleep</gloss>) is examined. There are various scriptural passages regarding deep sleep. In one place, it is heard: "When this person is asleep, having become fully composed and serene, and does not know any dream, then he is in the subtle channels (<term>nadi</term> <gloss>subtle energy channels</gloss>)." Elsewhere, after mentioning the channels, it is said: "Moving through them, he rests in the <term>puritat</term> <gloss>the membrane surrounding the heart</gloss>." Elsewhere, again mentioning the channels: "He is in them when, being asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one in the <term>prana</term> <gloss>the life force/the Supreme</gloss>." Again, elsewhere: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Elsewhere: "Then, O gentle one, he becomes united with the Truth (<term>sat</term> <gloss>the Supreme Being</gloss>); he has reached his own Self." And also: "Embraced by the omniscient Self, he knows nothing of the external or the internal."

There is a doubt here: are these—the channels and the rest—separate, mutually independent places of deep sleep, or do they form a single place of sleep, depending upon one another? 

What is the initial view? That they are separate, because they are mentioned with the same purpose. For things with the same purpose are not usually dependent upon one another in a context where...

48. As a result of this [there follows] speed [great as that] of the central-organ, action of the instruments of [knowledge] disjunct [from the body], and the subjugation of the primary-cause.

Speed of the mind means that the body acquires motion comparable [to that] of the mind. Action of the instruments of knowledge disjunct [from the body] is the acquisition by the discarnate organs of the fluctuation required for the place and time and object desired. Subjugation of the primary cause is the mastery over all evolving causes and evolved effects. These three perfections are called Honey-Faced (rnadhupratika). And they are acquired as the result of the subjugation in five forms of instruments [of perception].

He describes the perfections which result from the subjugation, in five kinds, of the organs. 48. As a result of this .... and the subjugation. The fact that the organs are instruments [of perception] even for the discarnate is described as being the action of the instruments [of perception] disjunct [from the body].

The place is Kashmir or some other [place]. The time is the past or some other [time]. The object is subtile or other. As a result of the subjugation of the organ and of the inherence, [there follows] mastery of all evolving-causes and evolved-effects, a subjugation of the primary cause. These perfections are called Honey- Faced by those persons who are expert in the yoga system. An objector says 'This may be true. By subjugation of the organs, the organs together with their objects may be mastered. But what is gained [by subjugation] of the primary cause and the other causes of these [organs] ? ' In reply to this he says «And they.» The instruments [of perception] are the organs. The five forms are [the five] processes-of-knowing [iii. 47]. [The result follows] from the subjugation of these. What he means to say is this : These perfections are not- a result of a subjugation of organs in general but of the five forms [of the processes-of-knowing]. And included in these [five] is the primary-cause and the rest.

49. He who has only the full discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self is one who has authority over all states-of-existence and is one who knows all.

He who is grounded in only the full discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self, and who is in the higher consciousness of being master in the higher clearness, and who has the sattva of his thinking-substance cleansed from the defilement of rajas and tamas is one who has authority over all states-of-existence. The aspects (guna) which are the essence of all things, which have both the determinations and the objects-of-determinations as their essence, present themselves as being the essence of the object-for-sight in its totality to their Owner, the Soul (ksetrajna). This is the meaning. — Being <one who knows alb refers to the [intuitive] knowledge, produced by discrimination and rising instantaneously [into consciousness], of the aspects (guna) which are the essence of all, whether they be [iii. 14] quiescent or uprisen or indeterminable. This is the meaning. It is this perfection that is termed [i. 36] the ' undistressed,' by attaining to which the yogin who knows all, whose hindrances and bondages have dwindled, takes his recreation as having mastery.

These same constraints, Which whether mediately or immediately lead to powers in the form of knowledge and of activity, are for the sake of the discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self by way of the confidence produced by grasping the perfections in turn and binding them together. The supernormal powers subsidiary to this [discernment] are shown [in the sutra]. 49. Sattva . . . and. There is clearness in so far as the defilement by rajas and tamas has been washed away. As a result of this there is the higher consciousness of being master. It was inevitable that the sattva of the mind-stuff should be overwhelmed by the rajas and tamas. But when the latter subside, it is this [sattva] that is to be mastered by the yogin its master. When it is mastered, the yogin who is grounded in only the full discernment of the difference between the sattva and the Self, is one who has authority over all states-of-existence. This same he explains by the words «essence of all things.»

<meta>continues from the previous discussion on the mastery of the senses</meta>

# From that comes speed of mind, perception without bodily organs, and mastery over primary matter. (48)

The attainment of unsurpassed speed of movement for the body is <term>manojavitvam</term> <gloss>speed of mind</gloss>. The attainment of the functions of the senses independent of the body, regardless of desired place, time, or object, is <term>vikaraṇabhāvaḥ</term> <gloss>perception without organs</gloss>. Mastery over all transformations of nature <note>original: prakṛti-vikāra</note> is <term>pradhānajayaḥ</term> <gloss>mastery over primary matter</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like reflections</gloss>. These are attained from the mastery over the five forms of the instruments of perception. (48)

# To one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the pure intelligence and the Self, belongs sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience. (49)

When the purity of the mind <note>original: buddhi-sattva</note> has its stains of passion <note>term: rajas</note> and darkness <note>term: tamas</note> washed away, and the yogi is in a state of supreme lucidity <note>term: vaiśāradya</note> and masterly consciousness, they stand firmly in the discernment of the distinction between the pure intelligence and the Self. At this stage, they gain sovereignty over all states of existence. All qualities <note>term: guṇas</note>, which constitute the essence of all things, become...

<column-break/>

He explains the accomplishments resulting from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, perception without bodily organs, and mastery over primary matter.** <term>Vikaraṇabhāvaḥ</term> is the state of the senses acting without the body. Place refers to regions such as Kashmir; time refers to the past and other periods; objects refer to subtle things and the like. Through the mastery of the senses in their generic form <note>original: anvaya</note>, one gains mastery over primary matter, which is control over all transformations of nature. These accomplishments are called the honey-like reflections by those expert in the science of Yoga. One might ask: if through the mastery of the senses, the senses and their objects become controlled, how does this relate to primary matter <note>term: pradhāna</note> and other causes? To this he says: **And these...** meaning from the mastery of the five forms of the instruments of perception, such as grasping and the rest. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not come from mastery of the senses alone, but from mastery of the five forms which include primary matter and its constituents. (48)

These meditations <note>term: saṃyamas</note> are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action. Having established faith by producing their respective accomplishments, he now shows the intermediate glories of that very discernment of the difference between pure intelligence and the Self for which the meditations are performed: **To one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the pure intelligence and the Self, belongs sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience.** Lucidity <note>term: vaiśāradya</note> arises from the removal of the stains of passion and darkness. Then comes the supreme consciousness of mastery. Indeed, when the mind-stuff is overwhelmed by passion and darkness, it is not under control; but when these are subsided, it comes under the control of the yogi who is a master. In that state of control, for the yogi established in the discernment of the difference between intelligence and the Self, sovereignty over all states occurs. He explains this further: **all qualities...**

Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras

## From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. The state of having disembodied senses is the attainment of the function of the senses in accordance with the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over the primal matter is the state of having control over all modifications of nature. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolized</gloss>. These are attained through the conquest of the five forms of the senses ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the sattva-aspect of mind, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience ॥ 49 ॥

For one who remains in the state where the pure conscious principle is distinguished from the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>the luminous or purity-aspect of mind</gloss>—which has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>—having attained the supreme clarity and the final stage of detachment, there is sovereignty over all states of being. All modifications of nature <column-break/>
The author speaks of the accomplishments arising from the conquest of the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter.** The state of the senses being disembodied refers to their capacity to function without the physical body. Place refers to regions like Kashmir and others. Time refers to the past and other periods. Object refers to subtle objects and so forth. Conquest of the primal matter is the state of having control over all modifications of nature through the conquest of the senses connected with them. These accomplishments are termed <term>madhupratīkā</term> by those expert in the science of yoga. One might ask: if the senses are conquered and become subservient along with their objects, what does this have to do with the primal matter and its causes? To this, he replies: **These are attained through the conquest of the five forms.** This refers to the five forms of the senses, such as grasping and others. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not arise from the conquest of the senses alone, but from the conquest of the five forms, which include the primal matter and its derivatives within them ॥ 48 ॥

These are the <term>samyamas</term> <gloss>concentrated practices</gloss> that are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action. By directly or indirectly establishing faith, they lead to the intermediate manifestations of that discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the <term>sattva</term>-aspect of mind, which is the ultimate goal. He explains: **For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the sattva-aspect of mind, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>. Following this comes the supreme state of detachment. The mind-stuff was previously overwhelmed by <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term> and was not under control. When these are stilled, the yogi who has attained mastery establishes the mind solely in the discernment between the pure conscious principle and the <term>sattva</term>-aspect of mind, leading to sovereignty over all states of existence. He clarifies this: **All modifications of nature...**

## From that, speed of mind, independence from the body, and mastery over nature || 48 ||

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. Independence from the body is the attainment of the function of the sense organs—regardless of location, time, or object—as desired. Mastery over nature is the power over all modifications of primordial nature. These three accomplishments are called the *madhu-pratīkā* <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolic</gloss>. These are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the senses || 48 ||

## Only for the one who possesses the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the self, there is supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience || 49 ||

For one whose intellect-consciousness is cleansed of the impurities of passion and inertia, who resides in the highest clarity and the supreme state of mastery, and whose firm foundation is solely the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness <term>sattva</term> <gloss>the luminous aspect of nature</gloss> and the Self <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>the conscious observer</gloss>, there is supremacy over all states. All selves are qualities, and the activity...

<column-break/>

The author presents the accomplishments arising from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **From that, speed of mind, independence from the body, and mastery over nature.** Independence from the body is the state of the sense organs being independent of the physical form. Location refers to places like Kashmir; time refers to the past and future; objects refer to subtle entities and so forth. Mastery over nature is power over all modifications of primordial nature, achieved through the mastery of the senses. Those who are expert in the science of Yoga call these accomplishments the *madhu-pratīkā* <gloss>honey-like</gloss>. One might ask: let the senses and their objects be mastered through the mastery of the senses, but what has this to do with primordial nature and its causes? The author replies: **These are [attained through the mastery of the five forms].** This refers to the mastery of the five forms of the sense organs, such as grasping. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not arise merely from the mastery of the senses, but from the mastery of their five forms, which include the primary causes like primordial nature || 48 ||

These are the means of achieving power in the form of knowledge and action. Through self-control, whether direct or through the succession of faith established by the attainment of these results, the author shows the intermediate manifestations of that discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the Self: **Only for the one who possesses the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the self, there is supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of passion and inertia. From that comes the supreme state of mastery. The conscious mind was previously subject to passion and inertia, but upon their cessation, it becomes subject to the yogi who has attained self-control. For the yogi established in this state, who has no other foundation but the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the Self, there is supremacy over all states of existence. The author explains this: **All selves are qualities...**

PEACEFUL LIFE.

Mazgusri, the prince royal, said to the Lord: It is difficult, Lord, most difficult, what these Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas will attempt out of reverence for the Lord. How are these Bodhisattvas MahAsattvas to promulgate this Dharmaparydya at the end of time, at the last period? Whereupon the Lord answered Mazgusri, the prince royal: A Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Mazgusri, he who is to promulgate this Dharmaparydya at the end of time, at the last period, must be firm in four things. In which things? The Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Ma#gusri, must be firm in his conduct and proper sphere if he wishes to teach this Dharmaparyaya. And how, Maggusri, is a Bodhisattva Mahasattva firm in his conduct and proper sphere? When the Bodhisattva Mahdsattva, Ma#gusri, is patient, meek, has reached the stage of meekness ; when he is not rash, nor envious; when, moreover, Mazigusri, he clings to no law whatever and sees the real character of the laws (or things) ; when he is refraining from investigating and discussing these laws, Mazigusri; that is called the conduct of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva. And what is the proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahdsattva, Mazgusri ? When the Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Ma#gusri, does not serve, not court, not wait upon kings; does not serve, not court, not wait upon princes; when he does not approach them; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon persons of another sect, Aarakas, Parivragakas, Agivakas, Nirgranthas, nor persons passionately fond of fine literature; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon adepts at worldly spells, and votaries of a worldly philosophy, nor keep any intercourse with them ; when he does not go to see KAndalas, jugglers, vendors of pork, poulterers, deer-hunters, butchers, actors and dancers, wrestlers, nor resort to places whither others flock for amusement and sport; when he keeps no intercourse with them unless from time to time to preach the law to them when they come to him, and that freely; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon monks, nuns, lay devotees, male and female, who are adherents of the vehicle of disciples, nor keep intercourse with them ; when he does not come in contact with them at the place of promenade or in the monastery, unless from time to time to preach the law to them when they come to him, and even that freely. This, Mazgusri, is the proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahdasattva.

Again, Maagusri, the Bodhisattva Mahdasattva does not take hold of some favourable opportunity or another to preach the law to females every now and anon, nor is he desirous of repeatedly seeing females ; nor does he think it proper to visit families and then too often address a girl, virgin, or young wife, nor does he greet them too fondly in return. He does not preach the law to a hermaphrodite, keeps no intercourse with such a person, nor greets too friendly in return. He does not enter a house alone in order to receive alms, unless having the Tathagata in his thoughts. And when he happens to preach the law to females, he does not do so by passionate attachment to the law, far less by passionate attachment to a woman. When he is preaching, he does not display his row of teeth, let alone a quick emotion on his physiognomy. He addresses no novice, male or female, no nun, no monk, no young boy, no young girl, nor enters upon a conversation with them; he shows no great readiness in answering their address, nor cares to give too frequent answers. This, Ma#gusri, is called the first proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

# 13. Chapter on Peaceful Practices

Then Manjushri, the crown prince of the Dharma, said to the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult, what these Bodhisattvas, these great beings, have endured out of respect for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should these Bodhisattvas, these great beings, teach this <term>dharmaparyaya</term> <gloss>discourse on the Dharma</gloss> in the final age, in the final time?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One replied to Manjushri, the crown prince of the Dharma: "Manjushri, a Bodhisattva, a great being, should teach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final time, by establishing himself in four matters. In which four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva, a great being, should teach this discourse on the Dharma when established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association. 

And how, Manjushri, is a Bodhisattva, a great being, established in proper conduct? It is when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva, a great being, is patient, disciplined, has attained the state of the disciplined, has a mind that is not fearful or terrified, and is free from envy. It is when a Bodhisattva, a great being, does not dwell on any phenomenon, and perceives the true nature of things as it really is. This lack of attachment and lack of conceptualization regarding these phenomena is called the conduct of a Bodhisattva, a great being, Manjushri. 

And what, Manjushri, is the sphere of association for a Bodhisattva, a great being? A Bodhisattva, a great being, does not cultivate, associate with, wait upon, or approach kings, princes, high-ranking royal ministers, or royal officials. He does not cultivate, associate with, or wait upon other sectarians, wandering ascetics, mendicants, or Jains; nor does he associate with people devoted to poetic or secular treatises. He does not cultivate, associate with, or wait upon those who hold the mantras of the <term>Lokayata</term> <gloss>materialist philosophical school</gloss>, nor does he enter into friendly discourse with them. He does not associate with outcasts, fowlers, butchers, swineherds, poultry farmers, hunters, meat-sellers, actors, dancers, wrestlers, or boxers. He does not approach the places of their entertainment. He does not enter into friendly discourse with them. If they should come to him, he may occasionally teach them the Dharma, but he does so without relying on them. 

He does not cultivate, associate with, or wait upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who follow the vehicle of the Disciples <note>the <term>Shravakayana</term>, or path of those seeking individual liberation</note>, nor does he enter into friendly discourse with them. He does not share the same sphere of activity with them, whether in walking meditation or in dwelling. If they should come to him, he may occasionally teach them the Dharma, but he does so without relying on them. This, Manjushri, is the sphere of association for a Bodhisattva, a great being.

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva, a great being, Manjushri, does not preach the Dharma to women by lingering on their attractive features, nor does he desire to see them frequently. He does not enter the homes of families, nor does he think it appropriate to converse frequently with young girls, unmarried maidens, or young brides, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not preach the Dharma to a eunuch, does not enter into friendly discourse with him, and does not exchange greetings with him. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, unless he is meditating on the recollection of the Tathagata. If, however, he does preach the Dharma to women, he does not do so even for the sake of Dharma-attachment <note>meaning he teaches without being seduced by the process of teaching or the interaction itself</note>."

<summary>In this chapter, the Buddha instructs Manjushri on the four methods of conduct and association for Bodhisattvas who wish to teach the Lotus Sutra during the difficult final age.</summary>
<keywords>Manjushri, Bodhisattva, Peaceful Practices, Dharma, Conduct, Sphere of Association, Tathagata, Shravaka</keywords>

Which four? In this regard, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva who is established in proper conduct and a proper sphere of activity should proclaim this religious discourse in the later times and in the final age. And how, Manjushri, does a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva become established in proper conduct and a proper sphere of activity?

When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva is patient, self-controlled, and has reached the stage of self-mastery; when his mind is free from fear, terror, or anxiety; and when he is not envious. Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva does not dwell upon any phenomenon <note>original: "dharma"</note> as it is, but observes the true nature of all phenomena according to their own characteristics. That which is non-clinging and non-conceptualizing regarding these phenomena is called, Manjushri, the proper conduct <note>original: "acara"</note> of a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva.

And what, Manjushri, is the sphere of activity <note>original: "gocara"</note> of a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva?
<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva does not associate with kings, nor does he associate with, attend to, serve, or approach princes, chief ministers, or royal officials. He does not associate with, attend to, or serve those of other sects, such as wandering mendicants <note>original: "caraka-parivrajaka"</note>, the <term>Ajivikas</term> <gloss>a deterministic sect</gloss>, or the <term>Nirgranthas</term> <gloss>Jains</gloss>. He does not associate with people devoted to secular poetry and literature, nor does he associate with, attend to, or serve those who hold to worldly materialist spells or the materialists themselves <note>original: "Lokayatikas"</note>; he does not form friendships with them.

He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, nor with boxers, pig-breeders, poultry-farmers,
<margin>N 181</margin>
deer-hunters, meat-sellers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not frequent other places of amusement or gambling belonging to others, nor does he form friendships with such people. Unless they approach him, in which case he teaches them the Law at the appropriate time, doing so without any ulterior motive.

He does not associate with, attend to, or serve those of the <term>Shravakayana</term> <gloss>the Vehicle of the Hearers/Disciples</gloss>, whether they be monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen; nor does he form friendships with them. He does not share a common sphere of activity with them, whether in the walking-path or in the monastery. Unless they approach him, in which case he teaches them the Law at the appropriate time, doing so without any ulterior motive. This, Manjushri, is the sphere of activity of a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva.

<margin>K 277</margin>
Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva does not repeatedly teach the Law to women by dwelling on the signs of attraction for one or another of them, nor does he constantly desire to see women. He does not frequent the houses of families, nor does he consider it appropriate to converse frequently with young girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them.

He does not teach the Law to a <term>pandaka</term> <gloss>eunuch or person of indeterminate gender</gloss>, nor does he form a friendship or exchange greetings with one. He does not enter a house alone for alms, except when he is practicing the mindfulness of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Gone One/Buddha</gloss>. If he should teach the Law to women, he should not do so even out of a passion for the Law, <note>text breaks off</note>

<summary>The Buddha instructs Manjushri on the four qualities a Bodhisattva needs to preach the Lotus Sutra in the future, focusing on proper conduct and avoiding distracting or worldly social circles.</summary>
<keywords>Manjushri, Bodhisattva, peaceful practices, proper conduct, sphere of activity, ethics, social boundaries, later age</keywords>

13. Chapter on Happy Conduct

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180
W 235
Then, the young prince Mañjuśrī spoke to the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult, what these bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas have endured out of respect for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should these bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period?"

When this was said, the Blessed One replied to the young prince Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva should preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, having established himself in four dharmas. In which four?

Here, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva should preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, having established himself in proper conduct and proper spheres of association <note>original: "ācāragocara" — conduct and range/sphere of activity</note>. And how, Mañjuśrī, is a bodhisattva and mahāsattva established in proper conduct?

When, Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva and mahāsattva is patient, disciplined, having attained the stage of discipline, with a mind that is fearless and unagitated, and free from jealousy; when the bodhisattva and mahāsattva does not practice <note>or "dwell upon"</note> any dharma, and observes the true nature of all phenomena <note>original: "svalakṣaṇa" — own-mark/individual characteristic</note>. That which is without grasping and without conceptualization in these dharmas, this is called the conduct of the bodhisattva and mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī.

<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
And what is the sphere of association for the bodhisattva and mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī? When the bodhisattva and mahāsattva does not associate with kings, nor with princes, nor with high-ranking ministers, nor with government officials; he does not serve them, frequent them, wait upon them, or visit them. He does not associate with other sectarians, wanderers, mendicants, or ascetics, nor with those who follow treatises on aesthetics, nor does he serve, frequent, or wait upon them. He does not follow or associate with those who hold the mantras of the materialists <note>original: "lokāyata" — a school of Indian materialism/skepticism</note>, nor does he serve, frequent, or wait upon them, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with them. He does not associate with those who handle corpses, nor with those who sell meat, nor with butchers, nor with those who raise chickens or pigs, nor with hunters, <margin>N 181</margin> nor with fishmongers, nor with actors or dancers, nor with wrestlers or boxers. He does not visit the places where others engage in sensual entertainment or play, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with them. If he happens to visit them, he preaches the Dharma to them from time to time, but he does so without relying on them.

He does not associate with followers of the vehicle of the disciples <note>original: "śrāvakayānīya" — followers of the lesser vehicle</note>, monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, nor does he serve, frequent, or wait upon them, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with them. He does not share the same sphere of activity with them, whether in walking or in dwelling. If he happens to visit them, he preaches the Dharma to them from time to time, but he does so without relying on them. This, Mañjuśrī, is the sphere of association of the bodhisattva and mahāsattva."

<margin>K 277</margin>
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva does not preach the Dharma to women by grasping at any sign of attachment, nor does he have a desire to see women frequently. He does not visit households, nor does he think that a young girl, a maiden, or a daughter-in-law should be spoken to frequently, and he does not engage in polite conversation with them. He does not preach the Dharma to a eunuch, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with him, nor does he engage in polite conversation with him. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of begging, unless he is dwelling in the mindfulness of the Tathāgata <note>original: "tathāgatānusmṛti"</note>. If, however, he preaches the Dharma to women, he does not do so with a mind of attachment to the Dharma."

<summary>This passage defines the "happy conduct" of a bodhisattva in the final age, emphasizing the necessity of moral discipline, avoiding worldly associations, and maintaining detachment in social interactions.</summary>
<keywords>Mañjuśrī, bodhisattva, conduct, mindfulness of the Buddha, social boundaries, Dharma</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: this text continues the commentary on the Vedic sacrifice and the protective nature of the ritual vessels.</meta>

...for the sake of one's own protection. May such a vessel <note>original: "camasa"</note> of yours, which is the means of consuming <note>food or sacrificial offerings</note>, never slip away from you during battle. The seer <note>term: rishi</note> who perceives the mantra says: "Carry that vessel forward."

### Hymn 58, Verse 5

I offer with speech, with hearing, and with the mind, the eye of the sacrifice, its beginning, and its face. 
May the gods, being well-disposed, come to this sacrifice extended by the All-Maker <note>term: Vishvakarman</note>. || 5 ||

Word-for-word analysis:
The sacrifice’s; eye; beginning; face; and; with speech; with hearing; with the mind; I offer.
This; sacrifice; extended; by the All-Maker; toward; gods; may they come; being well-disposed. || 5 ||

This verse has been explained previously <note>referring to Atharva Veda 2.35.5</note>. I offer the senses such as the eye and the mind in relation to the sacrifice; I make them devoted to it. The gods, acting as if they are of good mind <note>well-disposed</note>, should come to and attain this mental sacrifice which has been stretched out and expanded by the All-Maker <note>term: Vishvakarman</note>, the creator of the universe. This is the summarized meaning.

### Hymn 58, Verse 6

Those who are the officiating priests <note>term: ritvijah</note> of the gods, and those who are worthy of sacrifice, to whom the portion of the oblation is made; 
may all those gods, as many as they are, coming to this sacrifice together with their wives, rejoice in the light. || 6 ||

Word-for-word analysis:
Who; of the gods; officiating priests; who; and; worthy of sacrifice; to whom; oblation; is made; the portion.
This; sacrifice; together; with wives; toward; having come; as many as; gods; in light; may they rejoice. || 6 ||

Among the gods, those who are the officiating priests <note>term: ritvijah</note> are those who perform the sacrifice at the proper time <note>term: ritu</note>. And those who are worthy of sacrifice <note>term: yajniyah</note> are those to whom the sacrifice is offered. For both these types of gods, the oblation <note>term: havya</note> is prepared and given as their allotted portion. As many as there are gods of such measure, may those great gods, along with their respective wives such as Indrani and others, come to this sacrifice and rejoice; may they be satisfied by the acceptance of the oblation.

This concludes the fourth hymn in the seventh section <note>term: anuvaka</note>.

The hymn beginning with "You, O Agni, are the protector of vows" is used in the offering of clarified butter <note>term: ajya</note> or in the ritual of placing peaceful fuel <note>term: shantasamidhadhane</note> when there is a transgression or omission in the New Moon or Full Moon sacrifices. This is stated by Kaushika in the rules of the collection <note>term: Samhitavidhi</note>—

Atharvaveda Commentary [Hymn 58, Verse 5]

And for our own protection. May this cup of yours, which is the instrument of consumption, not slip away, may it not depart from the battle. The sage who envisioned the mantra says, "Carry it."

I offer the eye of the sacrifice, its opening, and its face, with speech, with hearing, and with the mind. May the gods, being well-disposed, approach this sacrifice spread out by the <term>Vishvakarman</term> <gloss>All-Maker/Creator of the Universe</gloss>. (5)

Of the sacrifice. Eye. Beginning. Face. And. With speech. With hearing. With the mind. I offer. This. Sacrifice. Spread out. By the All-Maker. Approach. May the gods. Being well-disposed. (5)

This stanza has been explained previously (Atharvaveda 2.35.5). I offer the senses, beginning with the eye, and the mind as being connected to the sacrifice, and I make them inclined toward it. May the gods, being well-disposed, meaning acting as if they have good intentions, approach this mental sacrifice—this sacrifice spread out by the All-Maker, the creator of the world—and may they reach it. This is the summary.

Those who are the officiating priests of the gods, those who are worthy of the sacrifice, and those for whom the sacrificial portion is prepared as an offering. May all the gods, together with their consorts, approach this sacrifice and delight in its brilliance. (6)

Those. Of the gods. Officiating priests. Those. And. Worthy of sacrifice. Those for whom. The sacrificial offering. Is made. As a portion. This. Sacrifice. Together. With consorts. Approach. Come. As many as. Gods. With brilliance. May they delight. (6)

Among the gods, those who are the <term>ritvij</term> <gloss>officiating priests</gloss> are those who perform the sacrifice at the proper time. Those who are <term>yajniya</term> <gloss>worthy of sacrifice</gloss> are those to whom the sacrifice is owed. For both of these groups of gods, the <term>bhagadheya</term> <gloss>share/portion</gloss>, in the form of an oblation, is prepared and given. May as many gods as exist, those who are great in their brilliance, come together with their respective consorts, such as <term>Indrani</term> <gloss>the wife of Indra</gloss> and others, approach this sacrifice, and find satisfaction through the acceptance of the offering.

Thus ends the fourth hymn of the seventh <term>anuvaka</term> <gloss>section/chapter</gloss>.

The hymn beginning with "You, Agni, are the protector of vows" is prescribed for use during the omission of the <term>darshapurnamasa</term> <gloss>new and full moon sacrifices</gloss>, in the offering of clarified butter, or in the peaceful depositing of sacred fuel. It is indeed codified by Kausika in the <term>Samhitavidhi</term> <gloss>ritual manual of the collection</gloss>—
