translations.T3:
Atharvaveda Commentary [Hymn 58, Verse 5]

And for the sake of protection. May this cup of yours, which is the instrument of consumption, may this battle not slip away, may it not depart. The seer who envisions the mantra says that they should carry it.

I offer into the sacrifice, which has the eye as its beginning and face, through speech, hearing, and the mind. May the gods, being of good mind, come to this sacrifice which has been extended by <term>Viśvakarman</term> <gloss>the all-creating deity/the creator of the world</gloss>. (5)

This verse has already been explained previously (A 2, 35, 5). I offer the senses, such as the eye, as being connected to the sacrifice, meaning I make them inclined toward it. May the gods, acting as if they are of good mind, come and reach this mental sacrifice which has been extended and spread out by <term>Viśvakarman</term> <gloss>the all-creating deity</gloss>. This is the summary.

Those who are the priests of the gods, and those who are worthy of sacrifice, and those for whom the offering is made as their portion. May all the gods, having come with their wives to this sacrifice, take delight in the splendor. (6)

Those who are the priests among the gods, who are the performers of sacrifice at the proper time. And those who are worthy of sacrifice, those who are to be worshipped. For both these groups of gods, the <term>havya</term> <gloss>oblation</gloss> is prepared and given as their <term>bhāgadheya</term> <gloss>allotted portion</gloss>. May all the gods, however many there are, being great in their splendor, come to this sacrifice along with their wives, such as <term>Indrāṇī</term> <gloss>Indra's wife</gloss> and others, and take delight, becoming satisfied by the acceptance of the offering.

Thus ends the fourth hymn in the seventh <term>anuvāka</term> <gloss>section</gloss>.

The hymn beginning "You, O Agni, are the protector of vows" is prescribed for use during the <term>darśa</term> <gloss>new moon</gloss> or <term>pūrṇamāsa</term> <gloss>full moon</gloss> rituals, in the event of an error, or during the offering of clarified butter, or during the peaceful placement of sacred firewood. Indeed, it is codified by <term>Kauśika</term> <gloss>the author of the Kausika-sutra</gloss> in the <term>Saṃhitā-vidhi</term> <gloss>rules for the collection of hymns</gloss>.

<summary>This page provides a commentary on verses 5 and 6 of the 58th hymn of the Atharvaveda, detailing the ritual significance of the sacrifice and the invocation of the gods and their consorts. It concludes with the end of the fourth hymn of the seventh section and a note on the liturgical application of a subsequent hymn.</summary>

तच्छरैरर्जुनो वर्षं प्रतिजघ्ने ऽत्यमर्षितः । विफलं क्रियमाणं तत्समवेक्ष्य शतक्रतुः ।
भूयः संवर्द्धयामास तद्वर्षं पाकशासनः ।
सोऽसृजद्वर्षं महावेगैरिषुभिः पाकशासनः । विलयं गमयामास हर्षयन्नितरं तथा । <margin>८२८</margin>
<margin>पाय</margin> तत उत्पाद्य पाणिभ्यां मन्दराच्छिखरं महत् । सद्रुमं व्यसजच्चक्रो जिघांसुः पाण्डुनन्दनं ।
ततोऽर्जुनो वेगवद्भिर्ज्वलिताग्रैः शिखण्डिभिः । शरैर्विध्वंसयामास गिरेः शृङ्गं सहस्रधा ।
गिरेर्विध्वंस्यमानस्य तस्य रूपं तदा बभौ । सार्कचन्द्रग्रहस्येव नभसः परिशीर्य्यतः ।
तेनाभिपतता दावं शैलेन महता भृशं । शृङ्गेण निहतास्तत्र प्राणिनः खाण्डवालयाः ।
इत्यादिपर्व्वणि खाण्डवदहनपर्व्वणि देवकृष्णार्जुनयुद्धे सप्तविंशत्यधिकद्विशततमोऽध्यायः ॥ २२७ ॥
॥ वैशम्पायन उवाच ॥ तथा शैलनिपातेन भीषिताः खाण्डवालयाः । दानवा राक्षसा नागास्तरवश्च वनौकसः । <margin>८२९</margin>
द्विपाः प्रभिन्नाः शार्दूलाः सिंहाः केसरिणस्तथा । समुद्विग्ना विसृज्युस्त्यान्या भूतजातयः ।
तं दावं समुदैक्षन्त क्रुद्धाश्चाभ्युद्यतायुधाः । उत्पातनादशब्देन सञ्चारित इव स्थितः ।
ते वनं प्रसमीक्ष्याथ दह्यमानमनेकधा । कृष्णमभ्युद्यतास्त्रञ्च नादं मुमुचुरुणं ।
तेन नादेन रौद्रेण नादेन च विभावसोः । ररास गगनं कृत्स्नमुत्पातजलदैरिव ।
ततः कृष्णेन महाबाहुः क्षेतेजोभास्वरं महत् । चक्रं व्यसजदत्युग्रं तेषां नाशाय केशवः । <margin>८३०</margin>
तेनात्ता जातयः क्षुद्राः सदानवनिशाचराः । निकृत्ताः शतशः सर्व्वे निपेतुरनलं क्षणात् ।
तत्रादृश्यन्त ते दैत्याः कृष्णचक्रविदारिताः । वसारुधिरसंपृक्ताः सन्ध्यायामिव तोयदाः ।
पिशाचानर्चिषे नागान् पशूंश्चैव सहस्रशः । निघ्नंश्चरति वार्ष्णेयः कालवत्तञ्च भारत ।
चित्रं चित्रं पुनश्चक्रं कृष्णस्यामित्रघातिनः । छित्त्वा नैकानि सत्त्वानि पाणिमेति पुनः पुनः ।
तथातु निघ्नतस्तस्य पिशाचोरगराक्षसान् । बभूव रूपमत्युग्रं सर्व्वभूतात्मनस्तदा । <margin>८३१</margin>
समेतानान्तु सर्व्वेषां देवतानाञ्च सर्व्वशः । विजेता नाभवत्कश्चित्कृष्णपाण्डवयोर्मृधे ।
तयोर्बलमपरित्रातुं तञ्च दावं यदा सुराः । नाशक्नुवन् शमयितुं तदाऽभवन् पराङ्मुखाः ।
शतक्रतुस्तु संप्रेक्ष्य विमुखानमरांस्तथा । बभूव मुदितो राजन् प्रशंसन् केशवार्जुनौ ।
निवृत्तेष्वथ देवेषु वागुवाचाशरीरिणी । शतक्रतुं समाभाष्य महागम्भीरनिस्वना ।
न ते सखा संनिहितस्तक्षको भुजगोत्तमः । दाहकाले खाण्डवस्य कुरुक्षेत्रं गतो ह्यसौ । <margin>८३२</margin>
न च शक्या युधा जेतुं कथञ्चिदपि वासव । वासुदेवार्जुनौवेतौ निबोध वचनान्मम ।
नरनारायणौवेतौ पूर्व्वदेवौ दिविश्रुतौ । भवानप्यभिजानाति यद्वीर्य्यं यत्पराक्रमौ ।
नैतौ शक्या दुराधर्षौ विजेतुमजितौ युधि । अपि सर्व्वेषु लोकेषु पुराणऋषिसत्तमौ ।
पूजनीयतमावेतावपि सर्व्वैः सुरासुरैः । यक्षराक्षसगन्धर्व्वनरकिन्नरपन्नगैः ।
तस्मादितः सुरैः सार्द्धं गन्तुमर्हसि वासव । दिष्टं चाप्यनुपश्यैतत् खाण्डवस्य विनाशनं । <margin>८३३</margin>
इति वाक्यमुपश्रुत्य तथ्यमित्यमरेश्वरः । क्रोधमर्षं समुत्सृज्य संप्रतस्थे दिवं तदा ।

The chastiser of Paka then caused a heavy shower of stones, desiring to ascertain the prowess of Arjuna who was able to draw the bow even with his left hand. Arjuna, in great wrath, dispelled with his arrows that thick shower. Then he of a hundred sacrifices beholding that shower baffled, once more caused a thicker shower of stones. But the son of the chastiser of Paka (viz., Arjuna) gratified his father by baffling that shower also with his swift arrows. Then Sakra, desirous of smiting down the son of Pandu, tore up with his hands a large peak from Mandara, with tall trees on it, and hurled it against him. But Arjuna divided that mountain-peak into a thousand pieces by his swift-going and fire-mouthed arrows. The fragments of that mountain, in falling through the skies, looked as if the sun and the moon and the planets, displaced from their positions fell down on earth. That huge peak fell down upon that forest and by its fall killed numerous living creatures that dwelt in Khandava.'"

SECTION CCXXX

"Vaisampayana said, 'Then the inhabitants of the forest of Khandava, the Danavas and Rakshasas and Nagas and wolves and bears and other wild animals, and elephants with rent temples, and tigers, and lions with manes and deer and buffaloes by hundreds, and birds, and various other creatures, frightened at the falling stones and extremely anxious, began to fly in all directions. They saw the forest (burning all around) and Krishna and Arjuna also ready with their weapons. Frightened at the terrible sounds that were audible there those creatures lost their power of movement. Beholding the forest burning in innumerable places and Krishna also ready to smite them down with his weapons, they all set up a frightful roar. With that terrible clamour as also with the roar of fire, the whole welkin resounded, as it were, with the voice of portentous clouds. Kesava of dark hue and mighty arms, in order to compass their destruction, hurled at them his large and fierce discus resplendent with its own energy. The forest-dwellers including the Danavas and the Rakshasas, afflicted by that weapon, were cut in hundreds of pieces and fell unto the mouth of Agni. Mangled by Krishna's discus, the Asuras were besmeared with blood and fat and looked like evening clouds. And, O Bharata, he of the Vrishni race moved able like death itself, slaying Pisachas and birds and Nagas and other creatures by thousands. The discus itself, repeatedly hurled from the hands of Krishna, that slayer of all foes, came back to his hands after slaughtering numberless creatures. The face and form of Krishna that soul of every created thing--became fierce to behold while he was thus employed in the slaughter of the Pisachas, Nagas and Rakshasas. No one among the celestials, who had mustered there could vanquish in battle Krishna and Arjuna. When the celestials saw that they could not protect that forest from the might of Krishna and Arjuna by extinguishing that conflagration, they retired from the scene. Then, O monarch, he of a hundred sacrifices (Indra), beholding the immortals retreat, became filled with joy and applauded Krishna and Arjuna. And when the celestials gave up the fight, an incorporeal voice, deep and loud, addressing him of a hundred sacrifices, said, 'Thy friend Takshaka, that chief of snakes, hath not been slain! Before the conflagration commenced in Khandava he had journeyed to Kurukshetra. Know from my words, O Vasava, that Vasudeva and Arjuna are incapable of being vanquished in battle by any one! They are Nara and Narayana--those gods of old heard of in heaven! Thou knowest what their energy is and what their prowess. Invincible in battle, these best of old Rishis are unconquerable by any one in all the worlds! They deserve the most reverential worship of all the celestials and Asuras; of Yakshas and Rakshasas and Gandharvas, of human beings and Kinnaras and Nagas. Therefore, O Vasava, it behoveth thee to go hence with all the celestials. The destruction of Khandava hath been ordained by Fate!' Then the chief of the immortals, ascertaining those words to be true abandoned his wrath and jealousy, and went back to heaven. The dwellers in heaven, O monarch, beholding the illustrious Indra abandon the fight, followed him with all their soldiers.

# The Burning of the Khandava Forest <note>Section 227 and 228</note>
## Adi Parva

Arjuna, becoming very impatient, countered that rain with his arrows. When <term>Shatakratu</term> <gloss>Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices</gloss>, the subduer of <term>Paka</term> <gloss>a demon</gloss>, saw his efforts being rendered fruitless, he further increased the downpour. The subduer of Paka sent forth rain with arrows of great velocity, causing a dissolution while delighting his own side. <margin>828</margin> Then, lifting with his hands a great peak from Mount Mandara with its trees, <term>Chakra</term> <gloss>Indra, the wielder of the discus</gloss> hurled it, desiring to kill the son of Pandu.

Then Arjuna, with swift, burning-tipped, crested arrows, shattered the peak of the mountain into a thousand pieces. The appearance of the mountain as it was being destroyed shone like the sky scattering away with its sun, moon, and planets. By that great mountain falling upon the forest, the creatures dwelling in <term>Khandava</term> <gloss>the forest name</gloss> were struck and killed by its peaks.

Thus ends the two-hundred and twenty-seventh chapter in the Burning of the Khandava Forest section of the <term>Adi Parva</term> <gloss>the first book</gloss>, concerning the battle between the gods, Krishna, and Arjuna.

***

Vaisampayana said: Terrified by the fall of the mountain, the dwellers of Khandava—the <term>Danavas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, <term>Rakshasas</term> <gloss>ogres</gloss>, <term>Nagas</term> <gloss>serpents</gloss>, and forest-dwelling trees—were distraught. <margin>829</margin> Mighty elephants, tigers, and maned lions, along with various classes of beings, abandoned their homes in agitation. They looked upon that forest fire, rising with weapons raised in anger; it stood as if agitated by the sound of uprooting. Seeing the forest burning in many ways, and Krishna with weapons raised, they let out a fierce roar. By that terrible roar and the roar of <term>Vibhavasu</term> <gloss>the Fire-god</gloss>, the entire sky rumbled as if with ominous storm clouds.

Then <term>Keshava</term> <gloss>Krishna</gloss> of mighty arms hurled his great, fierce discus, brilliant with the splendor of solar fire, for their destruction. <margin>830</margin> Those small species, along with the <term>Danavas</term> and night-wanderers, were caught by it; all were cut down by the hundreds and fell into the fire in an instant. There, those <term>Daityas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss> were seen being torn apart by Krishna’s discus, smeared with fat and blood like clouds at twilight.

The descendant of <term>Vrishni</term> <gloss>Krishna</gloss> moved like <term>Kala</term> <gloss>Time or Death</gloss> itself, O Bharata, slaying thousands of <term>Pisachas</term> <gloss>flesh-eating spirits</gloss>, <term>Nagas</term>, and beasts in the flames. Wonderful and marvelous was the discus of Krishna, the slayer of enemies; after cutting through many creatures, it returned to his hand again and again. <margin>831</margin> While he was thus slaying the <term>Pisachas</term>, serpents, and <term>Rakshasas</term>, the form of that Soul of all beings became extremely fierce.

Among all the assembled gods, there was none who could be the victor over Krishna and the son of Pandu in battle. When the gods were unable to protect the strength of those beings or quench the forest fire, they turned their backs. <term>Shatakratu</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>, seeing the immortals turning away, became delighted, O King, praising Keshava and Arjuna.

When the gods had retreated, an incorporeal voice of deep resonance spoke, addressing <term>Shatakratu</term>: "Your friend <term>Takshaka</term>, the best of serpents, is not present here; at the time of the burning of Khandava, he has gone to Kurukshetra. <margin>832</margin> Nor is it possible to conquer these two in battle by any means, O <term>Vasava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>. Understand these words of mine regarding Vasudeva and Arjuna. These two are <term>Nara</term> and <term>Narayana</term> <gloss>the ancient twin sages/deities</gloss>, the former gods famous in heaven. You yourself know what their heroism and prowess are. These two, unassailable and undefeated in battle, cannot be conquered even by all the worlds; they are the most excellent of ancient sages. They are most worthy of worship by all the gods and demons, <term>Yakshas</term>, <term>Rakshasas</term>, <term>Gandharvas</term>, humans, <term>Kinnaras</term>, and <term>Pannagas</term>. Therefore, O <term>Vasava</term>, you should depart along with the gods; see this destruction of Khandava as something ordained by destiny." <margin>833</margin>

Having heard these words and knowing them to be true, the Lord of the Immortals cast aside his anger and resentment and then departed for heaven.

<summary>Indra attempts to stop the burning of Khandava Forest by hurling mountain peaks, but Arjuna destroys them. Krishna uses his divine discus to slaughter the fleeing creatures, and a heavenly voice eventually persuades Indra to withdraw by revealing the divine identities of Krishna and Arjuna as Nara and Narayana.</summary>

Know this from my words: they are <term>Nara</term> and <term>Nārāyaṇa</term>, the ancient gods known in heaven. You also know their power and prowess. These two, who are difficult to conquer, cannot be defeated in battle, even among all the worlds; they are the best of the ancient sages. They are most worthy of worship by all—gods, <term>Asuras</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, <term>Yakṣas</term>, <term>Rākṣasas</term>, <term>Gandharvas</term>, humans, <term>Kinnaras</term>, and serpents. Struck by that, the lesser beings, along with the <term>Dānavas</term> and <term>Niśācaras</term> <gloss>night-wanderers/demons</gloss>, were severed in the hundreds and fell into the fire in an instant.
There, those <term>Daityas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, torn apart by Kṛṣṇa’s discus and covered in fat and blood, looked like storm clouds at twilight.
Slaughtering the <term>Piśācas</term> <gloss>flesh-eating demons</gloss>, the glowing <term>Nāgas</term>, and the animals by the thousands, the <term>Vārṣṇeya</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa (of the Vṛṣṇi clan)</gloss> moved about like Death itself, O descendant of <term>Bharata</term> <gloss>a title for the listener, Janamejaya</gloss>.
Wondrous, wondrous was the discus of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of foes; having severed many creatures, it returns to his hand again and again.
As he slaughtered the <term>Piśācas</term>, serpents, and <term>Rākṣasas</term> in this way, the appearance of the one who is the soul of all beings became most fierce. <margin>831</margin>
Among all the gathered gods, there was no one who could conquer Kṛṣṇa and the son of <term>Pāṇḍu</term> in battle.
When the gods could not protect their strength or extinguish that forest, they turned away.
Seeing the gods turn away, <term>Śatakratu</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>, the hundred-sacrificed one, became joyful, O King, praising <term>Keśava</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa</gloss> and <term>Arjuna</term>.
When the gods had retreated, a disembodied voice spoke, addressing <term>Śatakratu</term> with a deep, grave sound.
Your friend, the excellent serpent <term>Takṣaka</term>, is not present; at the time of the burning of <term>Khāṇḍava</term>, he had gone to <term>Kurukṣetra</term>. <margin>832</margin>
And these two, <term>Vāsudeva</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa</gloss> and <term>Arjuna</term>, cannot be conquered in battle by any means, O <term>Vāsava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>; understand this from my words.
These two are <term>Nara</term> and <term>Nārāyaṇa</term>, the ancient gods known in heaven. You yourself know their strength and prowess.
These two, who are difficult to assail and unconquerable in battle, cannot be defeated—even among all the worlds, they are the most excellent of ancient sages.
They are most worthy of worship by all: gods, demons, <term>Yakṣas</term>, <term>Rākṣasas</term>, <term>Gandharvas</term>, humans, <term>Kinnaras</term>, and <term>Pannagas</term> <gloss>serpents</gloss>.
Therefore, O <term>Vāsava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>, you should depart from here along with the gods. Observe that the destruction of <term>Khāṇḍava</term> is destined. <margin>833</margin>
Having heard this statement and realizing it was the truth, the lord of the immortals set aside his anger and resentment and departed for heaven.

<summary>This passage details the battle during the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, where Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna defeat the gods and their forces, ultimately leading Indra to accept their superior power and withdraw.</summary>

श्रीजयदेवभणितहरिमितम् ।
कलिकलुषं जनयतु परिशमितम् ॥ कापि० ॥ ८ ॥
विहरपाण्डुमुरारिसुखाम्बुजद्युतिरयं तिरयन्नपि वेदनाम् ।
विधुरतीव तनोति मनोभवः सुहृदये हृदये मदनव्यथाम् ॥५॥

रतिरणः तत्र धीरा स्थिरा ॥ ७ ॥ श्रीति । इदं श्रीजयदेवभणितं विपरीतताभि-(योग)क्रीडितं कलिकलुषं परिशमितं जनयत्विति शान्ति नयतु ॥ ८ ॥ तथाच सङ्गीतराजे ‘श्रीरागो यत्र रागः स्यात्तालस्तु द्रुतमुण्ठकः । वर्णनं वासुदेवस्य रतिस्तबलय्ये क्रियाः । पदेभ्यः पाटसन्तानं खरास्तेनास्तथैव च । प्रयोगश्च भवेद्यत्र स प्रबन्धवरः स्मृतः ॥ हरिमितचम्पकवर्णेभ्यः शेखराभिधःः’ ॥ इति हरिमितचम्पक-शेखरनामा चतुर्दशः प्रबन्धः ॥ इदानीं विरहातुरा राधा चन्द्रमुद्दिश्याह—विरहेति । अये कोमलामन्रणे । हे सखि, अयं विधुः हृदये अर्थात् मम अतिमदनव्यथां तनोति । किंभूतः । मनोभवः मदनस्य सुहृन्मित्रम् । मुरारेर्विहरहावस्थास्मरणेनाह । किंभूतः । विरहेण पाण्डुः यन्मुरारिसुखाम्बुजं तस्य द्युतिरिब द्युतिर्यस्य । अत एव वेदनां तिरयन्नपि आच्छादयन्नपि । एतदुक्तं भवति । पूर्वे मदीयविरहपाण्डुमुरारि-मुखकान्तिमत्वेन मम वेदना नाशयन्नपि कामसुहृत्त्वेन वेदनां करोत्येव । तदग्राह्यापि यदपेक्षया तस्य स्थितलाहुःखं नाभूतसांप्रतमन्यासक्तं तं ज्ञात्वा मया स्थातुं न शक्यत हंसलीलकः’ इति । ‘लवलेशकणार्णवः’ इत्यमरः ॥ ७ ॥ श्रीजयदेवेति । श्रीजयदेवेन भणितं यदरेः कृष्णस्य रतिरितं क्रीडितं कलेः कलियुगस्य कलुषं पापमर्थाच्छ्रोतृणां पाठकानां च परिशमितं जनयतु नष्टं करोतु ॥ ८ ॥ संप्रति चन्द्रोऽप्ययमधिकतरं व्यथयतीत्याह—विरहेति । अये इति विषादे । अयं दृश्यमानश्चन्द्रो मम हृदये मदनव्यथां कामपीडां तावदधिकं यथा स्यादेवं तनोति विस्तारयति । कीदृशः । विरहेण मद्विश्लेषेण पाण्डु धूसरं यन्मुरारेः कृष्णस्य मुखाम्बुजमाननपद्मं तद्युतिर्यस्य सः । तथा च । तादृशकृष्णमुखाम्बुजचन्द्रदर्शने कृष्णस्य मुखाम्बुजस्य स्मरणादति-व्यथा जायते इति भावः । किं कुर्वन् । वेदनामपि तिरयन्तिरोहितां कुर्वन् । तथा च । चन्द्रदर्शनेन तथा विवेकोन्मूलनं भवति कृष्णमुपायेन कृतापराधमपि तमेव मनः स्मरतीति भावः । व्याजनकत्वे हेतुमाह—मनोभव इति । मनोभवः कामस्य सुहृन्मित्रम् । तथा च निकटस्थितस्यापि कृष्णस्यानुसरणं मया न कृतमिति मदनाज्ञा-लङ्घनात्कामो मे वैरी जातः । सव्युस्तस्य साहाय्यं चिकीर्षता चन्द्रेणापि व्यथा जन्यत इति भावः । चन्द्रस्य कृष्णमनोजत्वेन कामस्य मनसिजत्वेनैव प्रसिद्धेः । सोदरत्वेन कामचन्द्रयोः सौहार्दत्वाच मनोभवपदेन कामस्योपादानम् । तथा च श्रुतिः ‘चन्द्रमा मनसो जातश्चक्षोः सूर्योऽजायत’ । इति । ‘वेदना ज्ञानदुःखयोः । भये क्रोधे विषादे च संभ्रमे स्मरणेऽपि च’ ॥ इति विश्वः । ‘तिरोऽन्तद्धौ तिर्यगर्थे’ इति च ॥५॥

Till at length, a fatal victress,
Of her triumph vain,
On his neck she lies and smiles there:--
Ah, my Joy!--my Pain!

But may Radha's fond annoy,
And may Krishna's dawning joy,
Warm and waken love more fit--
Jayadeva prayeth it--
And the griefs and sins assuage
Of this blind and evil age.

O Moon! (she sang) that art so pure and pale,
Is Krishna wan like thee with lonely waiting?
O lamp of love! art thou the lover's friend,
And wilt not bring him, my long pain abating?
O fruitless moon! thou dost increase my pain
O faithless Krishna! I have striven in vain.

<meta>continues from page 102</meta>

May this song, spoken by Sri Jayadeva about the <term>Hari-mita</term> <gloss>the measure or sports of Krishna</gloss>, cause the impurities of the <term>Kali Yuga</term> <gloss>the present age of darkness and strife</gloss> to be entirely pacified. <note>Refers to the eighth verse of the song</note>

Oh friend! This moon, a friend of the mind-born god of love, spreads intense pain of passion in my heart. Even as it masks my agony, it possesses the radiance of the lotus-face of Murari <note>Krishna</note>, which has turned pale due to the separation from me. <note>Verse 5</note>

### Commentary
The battle of love <note>original: <term>rati-rana</term></note> is described there as steady and firm. <note>Referring to verse 7</note> Regarding the phrase "Spoken by Sri Jayadeva": may this song concerning the reverse-posture love-play <note>original: <term>viparita-rati</term></note> bring about peace by causing the sins of the <term>Kali</term> age to be subsided. <note>Verse 8</note>

As stated in the <term>Sangita-raja</term>: "Where the melody is the <term>Sri-raga</term>, the rhythm is the fast <term>Munthaka</term>, the description is of Vasudeva <note>Krishna</note>, and the actions are like those of a blooming flower of love; where there is a sequence of rhythmic syllables <note>original: <term>pata</term></note> and musical notes <note>original: <term>swara</term></note>, that is considered an excellent composition." This completes the fourteenth song-composition named <term>Hari-mita-champaka-shekhara</term>.

Now Radha, distressed by separation, speaks regarding the moon: "Oh friend," <note>original: <term>aye</term>, a gentle address</note>, "this moon <note>original: <term>vidhu</term></note> spreads great pain of love in my heart." What kind of moon? It is a dear friend of the mind-born <term>Manobhava</term> <gloss>Kama, the god of love</gloss>. She speaks by remembering the state of Murari during their separation. The moon has a luster like the lotus-face of Murari, which is pale <note>original: <term>pandu</term></note> due to separation. Therefore, even though it covers or hides the agony <note>by its beauty</note>, it still causes pain. The meaning is this: previously, by having the splendor of Murari's face, which was pale from longing for me, it would destroy my pain. But because it is a friend of Desire, it now causes agony.

In the <term>Rasa-manjari</term> commentary: The words of Sri Jayadeva regarding the dalliance of Hari should destroy the sins of the <term>Kali</term> age for both listeners and readers. Now she explains how even this moon causes more pain. "Oh," <note>original: <term>aye</term>, used here in dejection</note>, "this visible moon expands the suffering of passion in my heart." How so? Its luster is like the lotus-face of Murari, which has become greyish-white <note>original: <term>dhusara</term></note> because of his separation from me. The idea is that seeing the moon, which looks like Krishna's face, triggers the memory of his face and causes extreme distress. What is the moon doing? It is "masking the agony." By looking at the moon, one's discrimination is uprooted, and the mind remembers only that Krishna, even if he has committed an offense. The reason for this pain is that the moon is a "friend of the mind-born." Since I did not follow Krishna even when he was near, I have disobeyed the command of Love, and thus Love has become my enemy. The moon, wishing to help his friend <note>Desire</note>, generates this pain.

Furthermore, it is well known that the moon is born from the mind, and the god of love is also "mind-born." They are like brothers. As the <term>Vedas</term> <gloss>ancient scriptures</gloss> state: "The moon was born from his mind, and the sun was born from his eyes." The word <term>vedana</term> refers to both knowledge and pain. The word <term>tiras</term> refers to disappearance or concealment. <note>Verse 5</note>

<header>Canto 7] Accompanied by the Rasikapriya and Rasamanjari commentaries 103</header>

May the love-play of Hari, as sung by Sri Jayadeva, bring an end to the impurities of the Kali Age. <note>8</note>

This moon, whose glow resembles the pale lotus-face of Murari <note>Krishna</note> during separation, though it attempts to conceal my pain, acts as a friend to Desire <note>Manobhava/Kama</note> and deeply intensifies the pangs of love within my heart. <note>5</note>

<note>The commentator notes: In this situation, the heroine is firm and steady. Regarding the verse beginning "Sri...", this love-play—or rather, the unconventional sporting—described by Sri Jayadeva should bring about the pacification of the sins of the Kali Age. As stated in the Sangeetarāja: "Where Sri-raga is the mode, the rhythm is fast, the description is of Vasudeva, and the acts are of intimacy, this is known as a superior composition." Thus, this is the fourteenth composition, known as Harimitachampaka-shekhara. Now, Radha, tormented by separation, addresses the moon: "O gentle one..." O friend, this moon actually intensifies the agony of desire in my heart. How so? It is a friend to Manobhava (Kama). It reminds me of the state of Murari's separation. How is the moon described? It possesses a luster like that of Murari's face, which has turned pale due to separation. Therefore, even though it hides the pain, it remains a friend to desire and thus causes pain. The meaning is: while the beauty of the moon, resembling Krishna's face in separation, should soothe my pain, its nature as a friend to Kama ensures it only increases my suffering.</note>

<note>Regarding the verse "Sri Jayadeva...", the play of the enemy of Mura <note>Krishna</note> as sung by Jayadeva should destroy the impurities of the Kali Age for both the listeners and the reciters. Now, the poet explains how the moon causes even greater distress. "O" is an expression of sorrow. This moon, which I see, expands the agony of love in my heart to an extreme degree. How is it described? It possesses the luster of Krishna's face-lotus, which has turned pale due to my separation from him. The implication is that seeing the moon, which resembles Krishna's face, causes intense pain through the memory of that face. What is it doing? It covers or obscures the pain. The arrival of the moon uproots one's discretion, causing the mind to remember Krishna, even though he has committed an offense. The reason for its deceitfulness is given: it is a friend to Kama. Since I did not follow Krishna even when he was near, and thus violated the command of Love, Kama has become my enemy. The moon, wishing to assist Kama, also generates this distress. The moon and Kama are well-known to be friends, as both are born of the mind <note>The text cites the Vedic source: "The moon was born of the mind."</note>.</note>

Canto 7] Provided with the <term>Rasikapriya</term> <gloss>a commentary on the aesthetic flavor</gloss> and <term>Rasamanjari</term> <gloss>a collection of aesthetic essence</gloss> commentaries 103

May the play of Hari, sung by Sri Jayadeva,
Cause the impurities of the <term>Kali Yuga</term> <gloss>the current age of darkness</gloss> to be pacified. (8)
This moon, mirroring the luster of Murari’s <note>original: "Murari" is a name for Krishna, meaning "Enemy of the demon Mura"</note> lotus-like face, pale from separation, even while suppressing pain,
Deeply expands the suffering of love in the heart, for it is a close friend of the Love-god. (5)

<note>The commentator notes the <term>rati</term> <gloss>love-play</gloss> within this context is characterized by the <term>dhira</term> <gloss>steady/composed</gloss> heroine. Regarding verse 8: This composition by Sri Jayadeva, detailing the reverse-love play, should destroy the sins of the <term>Kali</term> age. Regarding the <term>Sangitaraja</term> <gloss>King of Musicology</gloss>: Where the <term>Sri Raga</term> <gloss>a musical mode</gloss> is the melody and the beat is rapid, where the attributes of Vasudeva are described along with the actions of love, where the arrangement of the words and the melody are precise, such a work is known as a <term>prabandha</term> <gloss>literary composition</gloss>. The verse is identified as the fourteenth composition, titled <term>Harimitachampaka-shekhara</term>.</note>

Now, Radha, afflicted by separation, addresses the moon—<term>Viraha</term> <gloss>separation</gloss>, etc. 
"O friend, this moon expands the excessive suffering of love in my heart. It is the close companion of <term>Manobhava</term> <gloss>the Love-god/Kamadeva</gloss>. It reflects the luster of Murari’s lotus-face, which became pale due to separation. Thus, even while concealing the pain, it brings about suffering. The implication is: even if its appearance, resembling the face of my beloved, momentarily destroys my pain, its nature as a friend of desire only increases it. I cannot remain, knowing him to be elsewhere."

<note>Regarding verse 8: The sports of Hari, as sung by Jayadeva, shall eliminate the sins of the listeners and readers of the <term>Kali</term> age. Regarding verse 5: 'O' is an expression of lamentation. The moon expands the <term>madanavyatha</term> <gloss>suffering of love</gloss>. It is described as pale because of the separation from the lotus-face of Krishna. The sight of the moon, which reminds one of Krishna's face, creates excessive suffering. Why does it cause harm? Because it is the friend of the Love-god. Because I did not follow Krishna when he was near, the Love-god has become my enemy by order of my disobedience. The moon, wishing to assist the Love-god, inflicts this pain. As the moon is born from the mind, and the Love-god is also 'mind-born', they are brotherly in their alliance. The <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>Vedic scripture</gloss> states: 'The moon was born from the mind.' The term <term>vedana</term> refers here to the pain of knowledge and sorrow.</note>

<header>कथासरित्सागरः । [आदितस्तरङ्गः १००]</header>

भोज्यं महामांसमदायि तस्मै तृप्त्यै तदा सोऽपि तदाशु जग्ध्वा ।
तृप्तोऽस्मि नैवान्यदुपानयेति मामभ्यधान्मानुषमांसगृध्रुः ॥ ४९
कालं यदा नाक्षमतान्र किंचिदुत्कृत्य मांसानि तदा निजानि ।
प्रादामहं प्रीतिकराणि तस्मै योगेश्वरस्तेन स मेऽभ्यतुष्यत् ॥ ५०
अथाब्रवीन्मां स सखे दृढेन सत्त्वेन तुष्टोऽस्म्यधुना ते ।
तत्पूर्ववद्धीर भवाक्षताङ्गो वृणीष्व मत्तो वरमीप्सितं च ॥ ५१
इत्युक्तवन्तं तमहं तदैव प्रत्यब्रवं मां नय देव तत्र ।
यत्र प्रभुर्भे स मृगाङ्कदत्तो नातः परोऽन्योऽभिमतो वरो मे ॥ ५२
एतत्स वेतालपतिर्निशम्य मामभ्यधात्तार्र्हि ममांसपृष्ठम् ।
आरोह यावत्तरसा भवन्तं तस्यान्तिकं खस्य विभोर्नयामि ॥ ५३
इत्येव तस्योक्तवतस्तथेति स्कन्धाप्रमारोहमहं प्रसद्य ।
ततो वहन्मां स नभःपथेन प्रातिष्ठत प्रेततनुप्रविष्टः ॥ ५४
आनीय चेहाथ विलोक्य युष्मान्मार्गेऽवतार्याम्बरतश्च तेन ।
एतेन वेतालवरेण देव संप्रापितोऽहं तव पादमूलम् ॥ ५५
समागतश्च प्रभुणामहं गतः स चाप्येष समाप्तकृत्यः ।
इत्येष मे मानद नागपाशाद्वियुक्तस्य महानुदन्तः ॥ ५६
इति विक्रमकेसरिणो निजसचिवाच्छ्रुतवियोगवृत्तान्तः ।
मार्गे मृगाङ्कदत्तो गच्छन्कान्तानिमित्तमुज्जयिनीम् ॥ ५७
पारावतारुयशपाभ्रष्टक्रममिलितकतिपयामालः ।
मुमुदे स राजपुत्रः संभावितसकलसाध्यसंपत्तिः ॥ ५८

इति महाकविश्रीसोमदेवभट्टविरचिते कथासरित्सागरे शशाङ्कवतीलम्बके द्वात्रिंशस्तरङ्गः ।

त्रयस्त्रिंशस्तरङ्गः ।

नमो विघ्नजिते यस्य जानुदेशे विवर्तते । कुम्भस्तस्तेव नक्षत्रमाला रात्रिषु नृत्यतः ॥ १
ततः कथावसाने स मार्गमध्यात्समुत्थितः । मृगाङ्कदत्तो मुदितः प्राप्तविक्रमकेसरी ॥ २
गुणाकरेण सहितस्तथा विमलबुद्धिना । सविचित्रकथो भीमपराक्रमसमन्वितः ॥ ३
प्रचण्डशक्तियुक्तश्च श्रुताधिद्विजसंगतः । प्राप्तशेषान्विचिन्वानः शापविश्लेषितान्सखीन् ॥ ४
शशाङ्कवत्याः संप्राप्य प्रागेवोज्जयिनीं प्रति । गन्तुं प्रवृत्तः पुनरप्युच्चालात्मनाष्टमः ॥ ५
क्रमात्प्राप च स ष्मीमशुष्कतयामादपाम् । अटवीं चण्डमार्तण्डतप्तसप्तवालुकाम ॥ ६
तस्यां व्रजन्सचिवराजपुत्रो जगाद तान् । पश्यतौषाटवी कीदृग्दुर्गमायतभैरवा ॥ ७
एषा हि विघ्घटपथा जनलक्षा निराश्रया । उद्यद्‌भानलज्वालेवाभिमरुमरीचिभिः ॥ ८
विकीर्णरूक्षकेशैव तृणैरुच्छुष्कमर्मरैः । सिंहव्याघ्रादिवित्राससरोमाश्चैव कण्टकैः ॥ ९
रुदतीवातपक्षान्तजलाकाङ्क्षिमृगैः । तदेषा लरयास्माभिर्लङ्घनीया विशङ्कटा ॥ १०
इत्युचिवान्स तैः सार्धं सचिवैः क्षुत्तृषार्दितैः । द्रुतं मृगाङ्कदत्तस्तामटवीमुदलङ्घयत् ॥ ११
ददर्श चाग्रे सुमहत्स्वच्छशीतजलैर्भूतम् । सरोऽर्कतापगलितसामृतांशोरिव द्रवः ॥ १२

There I got hold of a corpse in the cemetery at night, and I washed it, and performed all the other necessary processes with regard to it, and I summoned a Vetala into it by means of that spell, and duly worshipped him. And to satisfy his hunger, I gave him human flesh to eat; and being greedy for the flesh of men, he ate that up quickly, and then said to me; 'I am not satisfied with this; give me some more.' And as he would not wait any time, I cut off my own flesh, and gave it to him to please him: and that made that prince of magicians exceedingly pleased with me. Then he said to me, 'My friend, I am much pleased now with this intrepid valour of thine, so become whole in thy limbs as thou wast before, and crave from me whatever boon thou desirest.' When the Vetala said this this to me, I answered him then and there: 'Convey me, god, to that place where my master Mrigankadatta is; there is no other boon which I desire more than this.' Then the mighty Vetala said to me; 'Then quickly get up on my shoulder, that I may carry thee rapidly to that master of thine.' When the Vetala said this, I consented, and eagerly climbed up on his shoulder, and then the Vetala, that was inside that human corpse, rapidly set out through the air, carrying me with him. And he has brought me here to-day, king, and when that mighty Vetala saw you on the way, he brought me down from the air, and thus I have been made to reach the sole of your foot. And I have to-day been reunited with my master, and the Vetala has departed, having accomplished what was required of him. This, O bestower of honour, is my great adventure, since I was separated from you by the curse of the Naga."

When Mrigankadatta, as he was going to Ujjayini to win his beloved, had heard, on the way, from his minister Vikramakesarin, this account of his adventures since he had been separated from him, that prince rejoiced, as he had in course of time found some of his ministers, who were separated from him by the curse of Paravataksha, and as he augured therefrom success in all that he had in hand.

CHAPTER C.

Honour to the vanquisher of obstacles, round whose knees, when he is dancing at night, there winds a garland of stars, which appears as if it had fallen from the globes on his forehead!

Then, the story being ended, the delighted Mrigankadatta rose up from the middle of the path, and set out again for Ujjayini for which he had long ago started in order to find S'asankavati, with a party of eight, including himself, having recovered Vikramakesarin, accompanied by Gunakara, and Vimalabuddhi, and Vichitrakatha, and Bhimaparakrama, and Prachandasakti, and the Brahman S'rutadhi, and he kept looking out for those of his companions separated from him by the curse of the Naga, whom he had not yet recovered.

And in course of time, he reached a treeless desert, all the water in which had been dried up by the heat, and which was full of sand heated by the fierce blaze of the sun. And as the prince was traversing it, he said to his ministers, "Observe how long, terrible, and difficult to cross is this great desert; for it has in it no refuge, it is pathless and abandoned by men; and the blaze of its fire of grief seems to ascend in these sandy mirages; its rough and dishevelled locks are represented by the dry rustling blades of grass; and its thorns make it appear to have its hair standing on end through fear of the lions, tigers, and other noisome beasts; and it laments in the cries of its deer exhausted by the heat and longing for water. So we must cross this terrible desert as quickly as we can."

When Mrigankadatta had said this, he quickly crossed that desert with his ministers, who were afflicted with hunger and thirst. And he beheld in front of him a great lake filled with pellucid and cold water, looking like streams that had flowed down from the moon after it had been melted with the heat of the sun. It was so broad that it filled the whole horizon, and it looked like a jewel-mirror made by the Fortune of the three worlds, in order to behold in it the reflection of herself.

He offered me great flesh <note>original: "mahāmāṃsa," referring to human flesh</note> for my satisfaction; I ate it immediately, and being satisfied, the one craving human flesh said to me, "Ask for no other boon." When I could not endure the time any longer, I sliced off my own flesh, which brings pleasure, and gave it to him. The <term>Yogeśvara</term> <gloss>Lord of Yoga/Master of Yogis</gloss> was pleased with me for that. 49-50

Then he said to me, "Friend, I am now satisfied with your firm resolve. Therefore, brave one, be whole-bodied as before, and choose from me your desired boon." When he said this, I replied to him at that very moment, "Lord, take me to that place where my master, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term>, resides; I desire no other boon beyond this." 51-52

Having heard this, the Lord of the <term>Vetālas</term> <gloss>vampire-like spirits</gloss> said to me, "Then climb upon my flesh-covered back; I shall quickly take you to that lord of yours in the sky." Upon his saying this, I agreed, saying, "So be it," and I climbed upon his shoulders. Then, having entered a ghost-body, he carried me and set out through the path of the sky. 53-54

Having brought me here, he saw you, lowered me from the sky along the way, and through this noble <term>Vetāla</term>, I was brought to the base of your feet, O Lord. Having met you, my master, I have reached my goal, my task completed. This is the great story of my separation, O bestower of honor, after I was released from the serpent-noose. 55-56

Having heard the account of the separation from his minister, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term>, while traveling on the road to <term>Ujjayinī</term> for the sake of his beloved, was filled with joy. That prince, having met a few of his followers who had strayed but then returned, and having obtained all possible success, rejoiced. 57-58

This is the thirty-second wave in the <term>Śaśāṅkavatī</term> <gloss>Moon-like/Having Moon-like beauty</gloss> book of the Kathāsaritsāgara, composed by the great poet, the illustrious <term>Somadeva Bhaṭṭa</term>.

The Thirty-Third Wave.

Salutation to the conqueror of obstacles, upon whose knee the necklace of stars revolves as he dances in the nights, like the pots on a water-wheel. 1

Then, at the end of the story, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term> arose from the middle of the road, having found <term>Vikramakesarī</term> filled with joy. 2

Accompanied by <term>Guṇākara</term>, <term>Vimalabuddhi</term>, the story-teller <term>Vicitraka</term>, and the valorous <term>Bhīmaparākrama</term>, along with <term>Pracaṇḍaśakti</term> and the learned Brahmin <term>Śrutadhi</term>, he searched for the remaining companions who had been separated by the curse. 3-4

Having reached the road to <term>Ujjayinī</term> to seek <term>Śaśāṅkavatī</term> before anyone else, he set out again, the eighth among them. 5

Gradually, he reached a forest, fearful with its dried-up riverbeds and sands scorched by the heat of the fierce sun. 6

Walking through it, the prince said to those ministers, "Look, how impassable and frightening this forest is. 7

It is a place devoid of paths, without people, and lacking any shelter; it is as if the desert mirages have become the rising flames of a fire. 8

With its dry, disheveled vegetation, its rustling dried grass, and its thorns that make the hair stand on end with the fear of lions, tigers, and other beasts, 9

it seems to be weeping with its deer that desire water at the edges of its dried-up ponds. Therefore, we must cross this vast, difficult forest quickly." 10

Having said this, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term>, along with his ministers who were afflicted by hunger and thirst, quickly crossed that forest. 11

In front, he saw a very large lake with clear, cool water, like the liquid essence of the moon melted by the heat of the sun. 12

He gave me great meat <note>human flesh</note> to satisfy him. I ate it immediately, and satisfied, he who craved human flesh said to me, "Bring no other food." 49
When I could bear the time no longer, I sliced my own flesh and gave it to him, for it brings him pleasure. The lord of the yogis <note>a powerful ascetic or supernatural being</note> was pleased with me for that. 50
Then he said to me, "Friend, I am pleased with your firm resolve. Therefore, be whole-bodied <note>restored to health</note> and brave as before, and choose from me a boon you desire." 51
When he said this, I replied to him then and there, "Lead me, O God, to the place where my lord, that Mrigankadatta, is. No other boon is desired by me." 52
Hearing this, the lord of the <term>vetalas</term> <gloss>vampire-like spirits</gloss> said to me, "Then climb upon my back, and I shall quickly take you to that lord of the sky." 53
When he said this, I agreed, and having climbed upon his shoulders, I set off. He, having entered the corpse-body, began to carry me through the path of the sky. 54
And having brought me here and seeing you, he lowered me from the sky. Through this excellent <term>vetala</term> <gloss>vampire-like spirit</gloss>, I have been brought to the root of your feet, O King. 55
I have arrived, and my lord, he who had completed his task, has gone. This is the great story of my separation from the <term>nagapasha</term> <gloss>noose of serpents</gloss>, O giver of honor. 56
Having heard this account of the separation from his minister, Mrigankadatta, on his way to Ujjayini for the sake of his beloved, traveled onward. 57
That prince, having met a few of his followers who had become scattered due to the loss of their path, rejoiced, possessing all his objectives within reach. 58

This is the thirty-second chapter of the Ocean of the Streams of Stories, composed by the great poet, the illustrious Somadeva Bhatta, in the Shashankavati Lambaka.

The Thirty-Third Chapter.

Salutation to the Conqueror of Obstacles <note>Ganesha</note>, upon whose knees the garland of stars revolves like a water-jar while he dances in the nights. 1
Then, at the end of the story, Mrigankadatta, having regained Vikramakesari, rose up from the middle of the road, joyful. 2
Accompanied by Gunakara, Vimalabuddhi, the one with diverse stories <note>Vichitrakatha</note>, and the one endowed with terrible prowess <note>Bhimaparakrama</note>. 3
Together with Prachandashakti and the learned Brahmin Shrutadhi, he searched for the remaining companions who had been separated by the curse. 4
Having previously obtained Shashankavati, he started out again toward Ujjayini, being the eighth in the group of the high-spirited ones. 5
Gradually, he reached a forest in the desert, scorched by the sun, where the water had dried up and the sands were burning. 6
Traveling through it, the prince spoke to the ministers, "Look at this forest, how difficult to cross, vast, and terrifying. 7
It is devoid of human paths and support, as if filled with the rising flames of fire in the form of desert mirages. 8
With dry hair scattered about, with dry, rustling grass, and with thorns that make one’s hair stand on end from the fear of lions, tigers, and the like. 9
It seems to be weeping with thirsting deer that look for water at the end of the quarters. Therefore, we must cross this vast, difficult place." 10
Having said this, Mrigankadatta, along with those ministers who were afflicted by hunger and thirst, quickly crossed that forest. 11
And in front, he saw a very large lake with clean, cool water, like the nectar of the moon melted by the heat of the sun. 12

Great human flesh was given to him for his satisfaction. After he had quickly devoured it, that creature, greedy for human flesh, said to me: I am not yet satisfied, bring more. 49

When I could no longer find anything, I cut off my own flesh and gave it to him to please him. By this, the Lord of Yoga <note>the Vetala or vampire-spirit</note> became satisfied with me. 50

Then he said to me: Friend, I am pleased with your firm courage now. Therefore, O brave one, let your limbs be uninjured as before, and choose a desired boon from me. 51

When he said this, I replied to him then: O God, lead me to the place where my lord Mrigankadatta is; no other boon is more desired by me than this. 52

Hearing this, the Lord of Vetalas said to me: Then climb upon my back. I will carry you swiftly through the sky to the presence of your master. 53

When he had spoken thus, I agreed and happily climbed upon his shoulders. Then, entering into a corpse-body, he set out, carrying me through the path of the heavens. 54

Having brought me here and seeing you all on the road, he brought me down from the sky. Thus, O King, I was brought to your feet by this noble Vetala. 55

I have been reunited with my lord, and his task is also finished. This, O honored one, is the great story of my release from the Naga-curse <note>the serpent's noose</note>. 56

Thus Mrigankadatta, while traveling on the road toward Ujjayini for the sake of his beloved, heard the story of the separation from his own minister Vikramakesari. 57

Having met a few of his ministers who had fallen into the sequence of the curse of the Naga Paravata, that prince rejoiced, seeing the potential success of all his goals. 58

Thus ends the thirty-second wave in the Book of Shashankavati in the Ocean of the Streams of Story composed by the great poet Sri Somadeva Bhatta.

# Wave Thirty-Three

Salutations to the Vanquisher of Obstacles <note>Ganesha</note>, upon whose knees the trunk circles like a garland of stars when he dances at night. 1

Then, at the end of the story, Mrigankadatta rose from the middle of the path, delighted at having recovered Vikramakesari. 2

Accompanied by Gunakara, Vimalabuddhi, Bhimaparakrama, Prachandashakti, and Shrutadhi the brahmin, and accompanied by the various stories, he set out. 3-4

Seeking his remaining friends who were separated by the curse, he proceeded again toward Ujjayini to obtain Shashankavati, traveling as the eighth in the group. 5

In due course, he reached a forest that was terrifyingly dry and waterless, with sand heated by the fierce sun. 6

As he walked through it, the prince said to his ministers: Look at how this forest is difficult to traverse, vast, and fearsome. 7

This path is broken, deserted by people, and provides no shelter; it is like a rising flame of fire with the shimmering mirages of the desert. 8

With its dry, rustling grass, it is like a woman with disheveled, rough hair; with its thorns, it is like one whose hair stands on end from the fear of lions and tigers. 9

With the deer longing for water at the ends of the parched regions, it is as if the forest is weeping. Therefore, we must cross this dangerous place with speed. 10

Having spoken thus, Mrigankadatta, along with those ministers who were tormented by hunger and thirst, quickly crossed that forest. 11

And he saw ahead a very great lake filled with pure, cold water, appearing like the liquid of the moon melted by the heat of the sun. 12

संप्रति संदिशति—

तामायुष्मन्मम च वचनादात्मनोपकर्तुं
ब्रूया एवं तव सहचरो रामगिर्याश्रमस्थः ।
अव्यापन्नः कुशलमबले पृच्छति त्वां वियुक्तः
पूर्वाभाष्यं सुलभविपदां प्राणिनामेतदेव ॥ ४१ ॥

तामिति ॥ हे आयुष्मान् । प्रशंसायां मतुप् । परोपकारलाध्यजीवितत्यर्थः । मम [ वचनात् ] वचनं प्रार्थनावचनं तस्मात् च आत्मनः स्वस्य उपकर्तुं च । परोपकारेणात्मानं कृतार्थयितुमित्यर्थः । उपकारक्रियां प्रति कर्मत्वेऽपि तस्योपकरोतीत्यादिवत्संबंधमात्रविवक्षायामात्मन इति षष्ठी न विरुध्यते । यथाऽऽह भारविः—'सा लक्ष्मी रुपकुरुते यया परेषाम्' इति । तथा श्रीहर्षश्च—'साधूनामुपकर्तुं लक्ष्मीं द्रष्टुं विहायसा गन्तुम् ।' इति । तथा च 'कचित्काचिद्वितीयादर्शनात्सर्वस्य तथा' इति नाथवचनमथावचनमेव । तां प्रियाम् एवं ब्रूयाः । किमित्याह—हे अबले तव सहचरः भर्ता रामगिरेश्चित्रकूटस्याश्रमेषु तिष्ठतीति—रामगिर्याश्रमस्थः सन् । अव्यापन्नः न मृत इत्यर्थः । अमरणे हेतुमाह—वियुक्तः वियोगं प्राप्तो दुःखी सन् त्वां कुशलं पृच्छति । दुःखादित्वात्पृच्छतेर्द्विकर्मकत्वम् । तथा हि सुलभविपदां अयत्नसिद्धविपत्तीनां प्राणिनां एतदेव कुशलमेव पूर्वाभाष्यं प्रथममवश्यं प्रष्टव्यम् । 'कृत्याश्च' इत्यावश्यकार्थे ण्यत्प्रत्ययः ॥

अङ्गेनाङ्गं प्रतनु तनुना गाढतप्तेन तप्तं
सास्त्रेणाश्रुद्रुतमुविरतोत्कण्ठमुत्कण्ठितेन ।

१ आयुष्मान्. २ ब्रूयात्. ३ एकम्. ४ वियुक्ताम्, नियुक्तः. ५ पूर्वाभास्यं सुलभविपदां प्राणिनामेतदेव, भूतानां हि क्षयिषु करणेष्वाधमास्यमेतत्. ६ सुतनु, तनु च ७ णास्रद्रवम्.

XXXVII
Say this, and she will welcome thee indeed,
Sweet friend, with a yearning heart's tumultuous beating
And joy-uplifted eyes; and she will heed
The after message: such a friendly greeting
Is hardly less to woman's heart than lovers' meeting.

XXXVIII
Thus too, my king, I pray of thee to speak,
Remembering kindness is its own reward;
"Thy lover lives, and from the holy peak
Asks if these absent days good health afford--
Those born to pain must ever use this opening word.

XXXIX
With body worn as thine, with pain as deep,
With tears and ceaseless longings answering thine,
With sighs more burning than the sighs that keep
Thy lips ascorch--doomed far from thee to pine,
He too doth weave the fancies that thy soul entwine.

translations.T1:
Uttaramegha.

Of those whose hair is parted <note>referring to young wives who traditionally mark their status by parting their hair</note>. "A woman whose hair is parted is a bride," according to the Amarakosha. [Brought by a friend] Having arrived, brought by a friend or through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is used to prevent any suspicion of infidelity. The news of the beloved is the news of the husband. "News, information, event, and report are synonymous with Udanta," according to the Amarakosha. It means that the news is slightly less than the reunion itself, but it is just as joyful.

Now, he delivers the message—

O long-lived one, tell her, by my words and for your own benefit,
Speak thus: "Your companion, residing in the hermitage of Ramagiri,
Alive and well, asks after your welfare, O helpless one, though separated from you;
For this is the first thing that must be spoken to living beings who are prone to misfortune." || 41 ||

Tell her. O long-lived one. The suffix 'matup' implies praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of performing favors for others. By my words, that is, the request, and also for your own benefit—that is, to fulfill yourself by performing a kindness for others. Even though the self is the object of the act of helping, the use of the genitive case 'atmanah' is not incorrect, as in phrases like "he helps him." As Bharavi says, "That is true fortune by which one helps others." Similarly, Sriharsha says, "To help the righteous, to see fortune, to travel through the sky." Thus, the statement of the master—that this is a second case of the same usage—is an unnecessary statement. Tell her, your beloved, thus. What should you say? He says, O helpless one, your companion, your husband, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, also known as Chitrakuta, is alive—meaning not dead. He provides the reason for not being dead: although suffering from being separated, he asks after your welfare. The verb 'to ask' takes two objects due to the state of being distressed. Indeed, for living beings who easily meet with misfortune, this very question regarding welfare is the first thing that must be asked. The 'nyat' suffix is applied here to indicate necessity.

With a slender body against a slender body, with a fevered body against a fevered one,
With eyes full of tears against eyes full of tears, with an unceasing longing against one who is longing,

1. Long-lived one. 2. You should speak. 3. One. 4. Separated, appointed. 5. This is the first greeting for living beings who are prone to misfortune; this is the first address for creatures whose instruments are prone to decay. 6. O slender one, and the body. 7. Flowing with tears.

Even though this acts as an object for the action of helping, the use of the genitive case 'atmana' is not contradictory, as it implies a relationship of intent. As Bharavi says: "That wealth is meaningful through which one helps others." Similarly, Sriharsha says: "To help the good, to see wealth, and to travel through the sky." This means he is not dead. He explains the reason for his remaining alive: separated and suffering from the separation, he asks after your welfare. Because the verb 'to ask' (pricchati) implies an object, it here takes two. Indeed, for living beings, whose misfortunes arise so easily, this inquiry about welfare is the very first thing that must be asked.

# The Latter Cloud <note>original: Uttaramegha</note>

<margin>The term for women with parted hair signifies married women whose husbands are alive. The Amarakosha <note>an ancient Sanskrit thesaurus</note> states: "Nari, Simantini, and Vadhu are synonyms."</margin>

Presented by a friend <note>original: suhṛdupanataḥ</note>; having arrived through the medium of a friend. The word "friend" is used to remove any suspicion of a deceptive message. The news of her beloved <note>original: kāntodantaḥ</note>; news is defined by the Amarakosha as "varta, pravritti, vrittanta, and udanta." It is slightly less than an actual reunion <note>original: saṃgamāt kiṃcidūnaḥ</note>, meaning it brings almost as much joy as the physical presence of the lover.

Now he delivers the message:

O Long-lived One, at my request and to do a favor for yourself, speak thus to her: "Your companion, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, being separated from you but still alive, asks after your welfare, O fragile one. For living beings whose misfortunes are easily met, this is the very first thing to be declared." (41)

Detailed explanation: O Long-lived One <note>original: āyuṣman</note>. The suffix denotes praise, implying a life made worthy by helping others. At my request <note>original: mama vacanāt</note> and to favor yourself <note>original: ātmanopकर्तुं</note>; meaning to make yourself successful through an act of charity. Although the self is the object of the act of favoring, the use of the genitive case <note>belonging to the self</note> is not incorrect, as seen in the works of Bharavi: "That wealth is useful which serves others," and Sri Harsha: "To favor the virtuous, to see wealth, and to travel through the sky." Thus, the grammarian Natha’s comment that the second case is seen elsewhere is merely a personal opinion. 

Speak thus to that beloved: "O fragile one <note>original: abale</note>, your companion <note>original: sahacaraḥ</note>, your husband, staying in the hermitages of Ramagiri <note>Chitrakoota</note>, being not dead <note>original: avyāpannaḥ</note>, asks after your well-being." He gives the reason for the inquiry: though suffering from separation <note>original: viyuktḥ</note>, he survives. This verb "to ask" takes two objects here. Indeed, for living beings for whom disasters are easily obtained <note>original: sulabhavipadām</note>, this inquiry into welfare is the very first thing that must necessarily be addressed. The suffix used here denotes necessity.

With his slender limb, your slender limb; with his scorched limb, your scorched limb; with his tearful limb, your limb flowing with tears; with his limb filled with constant longing, your longing limb...

<note>
1. Long-lived one. 2. He should speak. 3. One/Single. 4. Separated (feminine), Appointed. 5. This is the first thing to be said for beings whose disasters are easy; for in perishable bodies, this is the first breath. 6. O fair-limbed one, and slender. 7. Flow of tears.
</note>

<summary>The Yaksha instructs the Cloud on how to approach his wife, explaining that news from a friend is nearly as joyful as a reunion. He emphasizes the importance of inquiring after welfare as the first priority for those suffering in separation.</summary>

अखण्डितं प्रेम लभस्व पत्यु-
रित्युच्यते ताभिरुमा स्म नम्रा ।
तया तु तस्यार्धशरीरभाजा
पश्चाकृताः स्निग्धजनाशिषोऽपि ॥ २८ ॥

अखण्डतमिति ॥ नम्रा प्रणता उमा ताभिः सतीभिः पत्युः शिवस्य अखण्डतम् अक्षतं प्रेम लभस्व प्राप्नुहि इति उच्यते स्म अभिहिता । लट् स्म इति भूतार्थे लट् । तस्य हरस्य । अर्ध शरीरस्यार्धशरीरम् । अर्ध नपुंसकं इति समासः । तदजतीति अर्धशरीरभाजा तया गौर्या तु स्निग्धजनाशिषः बन्धुजनाशीर्वादाः अपि पश्चाकृताः अधरकृताः । ततोऽप्यधिकफललाभादिति भावः ॥

इच्छाविभूत्योरनुरूपमद्रि-
स्तस्याः कृती कृत्यमशेषयित्वा ।
सभ्यः सभायां सुहृदास्थितायां
तस्थौ वृषाङ्गागमनप्रतीक्षः ॥ २९ ॥

इच्छेति ॥ कृती कुशलः । सभायां साधुः सभ्यः । सभाया यः इति यप्रत्ययः । अद्रिः हिमवान् इच्छाविभूत्योः उत्साहैश्वर्ययोः अनुरूपं सदृशं यथा तथा तस्याः पार्वत्याः कृत्यं कर्तव्यम् अशेषयित्वा शेषं निःशेषं कृत्वा । समाप्येत्यर्थः । अशेषशब्दात्करोतीति ण्यन्तात् क्त्वाप्रत्ययः । सुहृदास्थितायां बन्धुजनाक्रान्तायां सभायां संसदि [ वृषाङ्गागमनप्रतीक्षः ] वृषाङ्कस्य हरस्यागमनं प्रतीक्षत इति तथोक्तः सन् । कर्मण्यण् इत्यण् । तस्थौ स्थितः ॥

तावन्भवस्यापि कुबेरशैले
तत्पूर्वपाणिग्रहणानुरूपम् ।
प्रसाधनं मातृभिराहताभि-
न्यस्तं पुरस्तात्पुरशासनस्य ॥ ३० ॥

तावदिति ॥ तावत् । यावद्गौरीप्रसाधनं क्रियते तत्काल एवेत्यर्थः । कुबेरशैले कैलासे । [ तत्पूर्वपाणिग्रहणानुरूपम् ] तदेव पूर्वं तत्पूर्वं तच्च तत्पाणिग्रहणं तस्यानुरूपं प्रसाधनं अलङ्कारसामग्री । आहताभिः सादरभिः । कर्तरि क्तः । मातृभिः ब्राह्मीप्रभृतिभिः सप्तमातृकाभिः । पुरं शास्तीति पुरशासनस्तस्य पुरशासनस्य । कर्तरि ल्युट् । भवस्यापि पुरस्तात् अग्रे न्यस्तं निक्षिप्तम् ॥

१ असो. २ क्ष्मात्. ३ बंधु. ४ आगमन प्रतीक्ष. ५ वरस्य. ६ स्मर.

Then at her mother's hest, the maid adored The spirit of each high ancestral lord, Nor failed she next the noble dames to greet, And give due honour to their reverend feet. They raised the maiden as she bowed her head: "Thine be the fulness of his love!" they said. Half of his being, blessing high as this Can add no rapture to her perfect bliss. Well-pleased HIMÁLAYA viewed the pomp and pride Meet for his daughter, meet for ŚIVA'S bride; Then sought the hall with all his friends to wait The bridegroom's coming with a monarch's state.

Meanwhile by heavenly matrons' care displayed Upon KUVERA'S lofty mount were laid The ornaments of ŚIVA, which of yore At his first nuptials the bridegroom wore. He laid his hand upon the dress, but how Shall robes so sad, so holy, grace him now? His own dire vesture took a shape as fair As gentle bridegroom's heart could wish to wear.

translations.T1:
<meta>continues from the previous section describing the bridal preparations of Parvati</meta>

You shall receive the undivided love of your husband. Thus addressed by those faithful women <note>the seven celestial matrons or wives of the sages</note>, Uma bowed low in humility. But she, who was destined to share half of his body <note>referring to the Ardhanarishvara form where Shiva and Parvati are joined as one</note>, soon surpassed even the blessings of her beloved kin.

<note>Commentary: The bowing Uma was told by the virtuous women, "Obtain the unbroken, perfect love of your husband Shiva." The word "shastra" used with "sma" denotes the past tense. Because she came to possess half of Hara's body, Gauri rendered the blessings of her affectionate relatives secondary. The implication is that she attained a fruit far greater than what their words had even envisioned.</note>

## Verse 29

Having completed every duty for her according to his desire and his vast wealth, the accomplished Mountain King <note>Himavat, the father of Parvati</note>, a noble man among the assembly, remained in the hall surrounded by friends, awaiting the arrival of the Bull-Bannered Lord <note>Shiva</note>.

<note>Commentary: The skillful Himavat, acting in a manner worthy of his intent and his royal power, left no part of Parvati's marriage rites unfinished. Having completed them, he waited in the assembly of kinsmen for the arrival of the one who bears the bull as his emblem. The term "sabhya" indicates his refined and righteous character within the courtly gathering.</note>

## Verse 30

Meanwhile, upon the mountain of Kubera <note>Mount Kailash</note>, the ornaments for the Wedding of the First Lord were placed before the Destroyer of Cities <note>Shiva</note> by the Divine Mothers, who had been summoned with great honor.

<note>Commentary: At the same time that Gauri's preparations were being made, the adornments suitable for that foremost marriage were laid out on Mount Kailash. These materials were presented before Bhava <note>Shiva</note> by the Seven Mothers, including Brahmi and others, who had arrived with reverence. Shiva is called the "Destroyer of Cities" here, referencing his victory over Tripura.</note>

<summary>Parvati receives blessings of eternal love from matrons while her father Himavat prepares the wedding hall. Simultaneously on Mount Kailash, the Divine Mothers prepare the bridal ornaments for Shiva.</summary>

translations.T2:
In the Kumārasambhava

"May you obtain the unbroken love of your husband," the women said to Umā, who bowed low. But she, having become one who shares half the body of him <note>referring to Shiva, who makes Pārvatī half of himself</note>, had already surpassed even the blessings of her affectionate kin. || 28 ||

Commentary: "Unbroken," etc. Umā, being humble, was addressed by those virtuous women who said, "May you obtain the unbroken, unblemished love of your husband, Shiva." The use of the imperfect tense is indicated by the particle *sma*. "Him," meaning Hara (Shiva). "Half of the body," meaning *ardhaśarīra*, formed by the compound *ardha* (half) in the neuter gender. By her, Gauri (Pārvatī), who has become one who shares half the body of him, the blessings of her dear ones were made secondary, or placed below, because she had gained a fruit even greater than those blessings.

The mountain king, having skillfully completed all the tasks befitting the desires and resources of his daughter, sat in the assembly occupied by his friends, waiting for the arrival of the bull-emblemed one. || 29 ||

Commentary: "Desire," etc. A *kṛtī* is one who is skillful. A *sabhya* is one who is worthy of the assembly. The mountain, Himavān, having completed every remaining task in a manner appropriate to the desires and wealth—that is, the enthusiasm and majesty—of his daughter Pārvatī, stood (remained) in the assembly occupied by his friends, waiting for the arrival of Hara, whose emblem is the bull.

Meanwhile, on the mountain of Kubera <note>Mount Kailāsa</note>, the accessories for decoration, appropriate for that former marriage ceremony, were brought by the Mothers <note>the seven divine mothers, such as Brāhmī</note> who had been summoned, and were placed before the City-Subduer <note>Shiva, the destroyer of Tripura</note>. || 30 ||

Commentary: "Meanwhile," etc. While Gauri's adornment was being performed, at that very moment, on the mountain of Kubera (Kailāsa), the items for decoration, matching that previous wedding ceremony, were brought by the Mothers who had been respectfully summoned, and were placed before the destroyer of the city (Shiva).

"May you obtain unbroken love from your husband," thus addressed, the humble Umā was told by those women. However, by her, who shares half the body of him <note>referring to Shiva, who shares half his body with Pārvatī</note>, even the blessings of her affectionate kin were surpassed. || 28 ||

"Unbroken," etc. Umā, being humble, was addressed by those virtuous women with the words, "May you obtain unbroken, unimpaired love from your husband, Shiva." <note>The use of the past tense marker 'sma' with the present tense 'uchyate' denotes a past action.</note> By her, the daughter of the mountain, who occupies half the body of him—that is, Hara—even the blessings offered by her dear relatives were made inferior, for she had already attained a reward greater than those blessings. || 28 ||

The mountain <note>Himālaya</note>, having skillfully completed all the duties appropriate to the wishes and the magnificence of his daughter, stood in the hall occupied by his friends, awaiting the arrival of the one who has the bull as his emblem <note>Shiva</note>. || 29 ||

"Wish," etc. The skillful one, worthy of the assembly, the mountain, having finished without remainder the duties appropriate to the desires and the wealth of Pārvatī, stood in the hall occupied by his kin, awaiting the arrival of Hara. || 29 ||

Meanwhile, upon the mountain of Kubera <note>Mount Kailāsa</note>, the ornaments suitable for the wedding were placed before the destroyer of the cities <note>Shiva</note> by the Mothers <note>the seven divine mothers, such as Brāhmī</note>, who had been summoned for this purpose. || 30 ||

"Meanwhile," etc. At the very time that Pārvatī’s adornment was being performed, on the mountain of Kubera, the wedding finery was placed before the Lord by the seven Mothers, who had arrived with reverence. || 30 ||

ऋक्षाः सिंहा वराहाश्च महिषा वारणा मृगाः । तेन शब्देन दिन्त्रस्ता जग्मुर्भीता दिशो दश ॥
शिखरं तत्त्रिकूटस्य प्रांशु चैकं दिविस्पृशम् । समन्तात्पुष्पसंछन्नं महारजतसंनिभम् ॥ १८
शतयोजनविस्तीर्णं विमलं चारुदर्शनम् । श्लक्ष्णं श्रीमन्महच्चैव दुष्प्रापं शकुनैरपि ॥ १९
मनसापि दुरारोहं किं पुनः कर्मणा जनैः । निविष्टा तत्र शिखरे लङ्का रावणपालिता ॥ २०
शतयोजनविस्तीर्णा त्रिंशद्योजनआयता । सा पुरी गोपुरैरुच्चैः पाण्डराम्बुदसंनिभैः ॥ २१
काञ्चनेन च सालेन राजतेन च शोभिता । प्रासादैश्च विमानैश्च लङ्का परमभूषिता ॥ २२
घनैरिवातपापाये मध्यं वैणवमं पदम् । यस्यां स्तम्भसहस्रेण प्रासादः समलंकृतः ॥ २३
कैलासशिखराकारो दृश्यते स्मिवोल्लिवन् । चैत्यः स राक्षसेन्द्रस्य बभूव पुरभूषणम् ॥ २४
शतेन रक्षसां नित्यं यः समग्रेण दृश्यते । मनोज्ञां काननवतां पर्वतैरुपशोभिताम् ॥ २५
नानाधातुविचित्रैश्च उद्यानैरुपशोभिताम् । नानाविहगसंघुष्टां नानागणनिषेविताम् ॥ २६
नानाकुसुमसंछन्नां नाना राक्षससेविताम् । तां समृद्धां समुद्रार्थां लक्ष्मीवाँल्लक्ष्मणाग्रजः ॥ २७
रावणस्य पुरीं रामो ददर्श सह वानरैः । तां महागृहसंबाधां दृष्ट्वा लक्ष्मणपूर्वजः ॥ २८
नगरीममरप्रख्यां विस्मयं प्राप वीर्यवान् ॥

तां रत्नपूर्णां बहुसंविधानां प्रासादमालाभिरलंकृतां च ।
पुरीं महायन्त्रकवाटमुख्यां ददर्श रामो महता बलेन ॥ २९

इत्यार्षे श्रीमद्रामायणे वाल्मीकीये आदिकाव्ये चतुर्विंशतिसहस्रिकायां संहितायाम्

### चत्वारिंशः सर्गः
**रावणसुग्रीवनियुद्धम्**

ततो रामः सुवेलाग्रं योजनद्वयमण्डलम । आरुरोह सुग्रीवा हरियूथपसंवृतः ॥ १
स्थित्वा मुहूर्तं तत्रैव दिशो दश विलोकयन् । त्रिकूटशिखरे रम्ये निर्मितां विश्वकर्मणा ॥ २
ददर्श लङ्कां सुन्यस्तां रम्यकाननशोभिताम् । तस्यां गोपुरशृङ्गस्थं राक्षसेन्द्रं दुरासदम् ॥ ३
श्वेतचामरपर्यन्तं विजयच्छत्रशोभितम् । रक्तचन्दनसंलिप्तं रत्नाभरणभूषितम् ॥ ४
नीलजीमूतसंकाशं हेमच्छादिताम्बरम् । ऐरावतविपाणामैरुत्कृष्टकिणवक्षसम् ॥ ५
शशलोहिनरागेण संवीतं रक्तवाससा । सन्ध्यातापेन संवीतं मेघराशिमिवाम्बरे ॥ ६
पश्यतां वानरेन्द्राणां राघवस्यापि पश्यतः । दर्शनाद्राक्षसेन्द्रस्य सुग्रीवः सहसोत्थितः ॥ ७

<note>१. इदमर्धम् क. नास्ति ।</note>

And they, endowed with great impetuosity, went on, oppressing the earth with their battle-array; and clouds of dust suddenly arose from the the march of the soldiery. And bears, and lions, and buffaloes, and elephants, and deer, and birds, overwhelmed with affright, made for the ten cardinal points. The graceful and lovely summit of Trikuta was entire, elevated, sky-piercing, of golden splendour, measuring an hundred yoyanas, clear-shining, level, inaccessible even to fowls, and incapable of being ascended even in thought—not to say of actual ascension by people. Lanka, ruled by Ravana, was situated on its top,—ten yoyanas in width and twenty in length. And that city was graced with lofty ornamented gateways resembling pale clouds, and golden and silvern walls; and Lanka was adorned with palaces and piles; like the sky graced with clouds on the approach of the rainy season. And that palace, which was adorned with thousands of pillars, and which, as if piercing the heavens, looked like a peak of Kailaça—was the residence of the Sovereign of the Rakshasas—the ornament of the city, (ever guarded by full hundreds of Rakshasas. And Lakshmana's auspicious and puissant elder brother, beholding that flourishing and wealthy city resembling the celestial regions,—charming to the mind, made of gold, graced with mountains, and decked out with mountains containing various metals,—resonant with the notes of various birds; abounding in various beasts,—furnished with various kinds of flowers,—and inhabited by various orders of Rakshasas,—was struck with astonishment. And Rama, surrounded by his mighty forces, saw that palace, filled with diverse kinds of gems, adorned with rows of edifices, and having huge engines and gateways.

SECTION XL.

Then Rama, accompanied by the monkey-leaders, along with Sugriva, ascended the top of Suvela, measuring a circumference of two yoyanas. And staying there for a while and looking at the ten cardinal points, he saw Lanka finely placed on the charming summit of Trikuta,—graced with elegant groves; and (he also saw) the unconquerable lord of Rakshasas, stationed at the top of the gateway, fanned with white chamaras; graced with the umbrella betokening victory; smeared with red sandal; adorned in red ornaments; resembling masses of sable clouds; and apparelled in golden attire,—his breast bearing scars from the tusk-ends of Airavata; covered with a sheet hued like the blood of hares; and appearing like clouds lighted up by the evening sun. And on seeing the Rakshasa-chief, Sugriva suddenly rose up in the sight of the lords of monkeys as well as Raghava. And influenced by wrath, he, mustering strength and vigor, rising from the brow of the mountain, bounded to the gateway.

# The Beautiful City of Lanka
### From the War Book of the Valmiki Ramayana

The bears, lions, boars, buffaloes, elephants, and deer were terrified by that sound and fled in fear in all ten directions. There was a single, lofty peak of Mount Trikuta that touched the sky, covered all over with flowers and shining like great silver. It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> <gloss>a measurement of distance, roughly eight miles</gloss> wide, pure and beautiful to behold. It was smooth, majestic, and massive, unreachable even by birds. It was difficult to ascend even in thought, let alone by the actions of men. Situated upon that peak was the city of Lanka, ruled by Ravana. 

It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> wide and thirty <term>yojanas</term> long. That city was adorned with high gateways that looked like white clouds. It was beautified by a golden wall and a silver wall, and Lanka was highly decorated with palaces and celestial mansions. Like the sky at the end of the hot season filled with clouds, the city stood grand. There, a palace decorated with a thousand pillars stood out, resembling the peak of Mount Kailasa and appearing to scrape the sky. This <term>caitya</term> <gloss>shrine or sacred palace</gloss> of the Lord of the Rakshasas was the jewel of the city. 

It was constantly guarded by a full hundred Rakshasas. Rama, the prosperous elder brother of Lakshmana, together with the monkeys, beheld that charming city of Ravana, which possessed many forests, was graced by mountains of various colorful minerals, and adorned with gardens. It was filled with the songs of various birds and frequented by various groups of beings. It was covered with various flowers and inhabited by various Rakshasas. Seeing that city, crowded with great houses and resembling the city of the gods, the heroic elder brother of Lakshmana was filled with wonder.

Rama, with his great army, gazed upon that city filled with gems, possessing many arrangements, decorated with rows of palaces, and featuring great mechanical engines at its main gates.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled The Sight of Lanka, in the War Book of the glorious Ramayana of Valmiki, the first epic poem, a collection of twenty-four thousand verses.

---

### Chapter 40
**The Duel Between Ravana and Sugriva**

Then Rama, surrounded by Sugriva and the leaders of the monkey troops, climbed the peak of Mount Suvela, which had a circumference of two <term>yojanas</term>. Standing there for a moment and looking in all ten directions, he saw the well-constructed city of Lanka on the lovely peak of Trikuta, built by Vishvakarman <note>the divine architect of the gods</note> and graced by beautiful forests. 

On a tower of the gateway, he saw the invincible Lord of the Rakshasas. He was flanked by white fly-whisks and graced by a victorious parasol. He was anointed with red sandalwood and adorned with jeweled ornaments. Appearing like a dark rain-cloud, he wore garments embroidered with gold. His chest bore prominent scars from the tusks of Airavata <note>the divine elephant of Indra</note>. He was wrapped in a red robe with the hue of a rabbit's blood, looking like a mass of clouds in the sky illuminated by the heat of the twilight. 

As the leaders of the monkeys and Rama were watching, Sugriva suddenly sprang up at the sight of the Lord of the Rakshasas.

<margin>1. This half-verse is missing in some versions.</margin>

<summary>Rama and his army arrive at Mount Suvela and view the magnificent city of Lanka. Upon spotting Ravana standing on his palace gateway, the monkey king Sugriva impulsively leaps into action.</summary>
<keywords>Lanka, Ravana, Rama, Sugriva, Trikuta, Suvela, architecture, fortifications, Rakshasa</keywords>

It was beautified by gardens variegated with various minerals, resonant with diverse birds, and inhabited by various classes of beings. 
Covered in various flowers and served by various demons, that prosperous city, surrounded by the ocean, was beheld by Rama, the elder brother of Lakshmana, along with the monkeys. ### Fortieth Chapter
**The Combat Between Ravana and Sugriva**

Then Rama, surrounded by Sugriva and the leaders of the monkeys, ascended the two-yojana plateau of Suvela. 1
Having stayed there for a moment, looking at the ten directions, he beheld Lanka, which was built by Vishvakarma upon the beautiful peak of Trikuta, well-laid out and shining with pleasant forests. He was surrounded by white chowries, adorned with a victory umbrella, anointed with red sandalwood, and decorated with jeweled ornaments. 4

He was wrapped in a red cloth, the color of a rabbit's blood <note>a shade of reddish-brown</note>, appearing like a mass of clouds in the sky surrounded by the glow of twilight. 6
As the monkey chiefs watched, and as Raghava <note>Rama</note> also looked on, Sugriva suddenly sprang up upon seeing the lord of the demons. 7

reference: For here these groups of gods are entering into you. Some being afraid are praying with joined hands, and the groups of great sages and Siddhas are saying 'Welfare!' and praising you with abundant (hymns) of praise. The Rudras, and Adityas, the Vasus, the Sadhyas, the Visvas, the two Asvins, the Maruts, and the Ushmapas, and the groups of Gandharvas, Yakshas, demons, and Siddhas are all looking at you amazed. Seeing your mighty form, with many mouths and eyes, with many arms, thighs, and feet, with many stomachs, and fearful with many jaws, all people, and I likewise, are much alarmed, O you of mighty arms! Seeing you, O Vishnu! touching the skies, radiant, possessed of many hues, with a gaping mouth, and with large blazing eyes, I am much alarmed in my inmost self, and feel no courage, no tranquillity. And seeing your mouths terrible by the jaws, and resembling the fire of destruction, I cannot recognise the (various) directions, I feel no comfort. Be gracious, O lord of gods! who pervadest the universe. And all these sons of Dhritarâshtra, together with all the bands of kings, and Bhishma and Drona, and this charioteer's son likewise, together with our principal warriors also, are rapidly entering your mouths, fearful and horrific by (reason of your) jaws. And some with their heads smashed are seen (to be) stuck in the spaces between the teeth. As the many rapid currents of a river's waters run towards the sea alone, so do these heroes of the human world enter your mouths blazing all round. As butterflies, with increased velocity, enter a blazing fire to their destruction, so too do these people enter your mouths with increased velocity (only) to their destruction. Swallowing all these people, you are licking them over and over again from all sides, with your blazing mouths. Your fierce splendours, O Vishnu! filling the whole universe with (their) effulgence, are heating it.

To this we reply as follows.

We must assume that the whole passage aims at intimating only that the person is higher than everything. Any information as to the relative superiority of the preceding members of the series would be devoid of all purpose ; for of the knowledge derived from such observation a use is neither to be seen nor declared by scripture. Of the knowledge, on the other hand, of the person being higher than the senses and everything else, raised above all evil, we do see a purpose, viz. the accomplishment of final release. And so scripture also says, ' He who has perceived that is freed from the jaws of death' (I, 3, 15). Moreover, the text by declaring that nothing is higher than the person and that he is the highest goal intimates reverence for the person, and thereby shows that the whole series of objects is enumerated only to the end of giving information about the person. — ' For the purpose of pious meditation,' i.e. for the purpose of perfect knowledge which has pious meditation for its antecedent. For the passage under consideration does not teach pious meditation by itself.

15. And on account of the word ' Self.'

The above conclusion is confirmed by the circumstance that the person under discussion is called the Self in I, 3, 12, 'That Self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth, but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect.' From this we conclude that the text wishes to represent the other beings enumerated as the Non-Self. The passage quoted, moreover, indicates that the person is hard to know, and to be reached by sharp minds only. — Again, the passage (I, 3, 13), 'A wise man should keep down speech and mind,' enjoins pious meditation as a means of the knowledge of the highest person, as we have explained under I, 4, i. — It thus follows that scripture indicates various excellences in the case of the purusha only, and not in that of the other beings enumerated.— The passage, moreover, ' He reaches the end of his journey and that is the highest place of Vish/m,' suggests the question as to who is the end of the journey and so on, and we therefore conclude that the enumeration of the senses, objects, &c., has merely the purpose of teaching the highest place of Vish;/u (not of teaching anything about the relation of the senses, objects, and so on).
